BasePK: 3033005

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, I see no contradiction in what the hon. member for Yukon says. He tried
The Territories
to present a certain matter as constituting a difference of opinion between members of the Liberal caucus and the government.
In my opinion the hon. member's motion calls on the federal government to commit itself to a policy which is already being implemented, and which began to be implemented some years ago.

BasePK: 3033007

Speech:
In my view the fact that the standing committe motion was adopted unanimously confirms that the present government's policy has received the agreement of all parties. However, although we may all agree on the principle of constitutional development for the two territories, we may differ on the methods of arriving at the same objective.
While the hon. member for Yukon is in a hurry and appears, at least in theory, to be favouring a rather "go-go" approach leading to a sudden change, not to say a break in the continuity of the evolutionary approach, the present government has opted for a more progressive approach which will permit it to avoid the drawbacks inevitably linked to rapid change. I shall have the opportunity to develop this point later, if time permits.
For the time being I wish to concentrate on the achievements of the government in recent years regarding the constitutional development of territorial government. I said a few moments ago that the government adopted a progressive approach. Because of that the government has been accused of being colonial and paternalistic, for example, by various theorists who dream about great principles but forget about the practical aspects, the vital needs of the population concerned. We must not forget these. On the other hand it is false to say that the progressive approach we have taken has been the equivalent of maintaining the status quo. To suggest that the situation has not changed extensively in the last ten years is unfair.
I remind my colleagues in this House that only ten years ago there was no territorial government of the Northwest Territories as we know it today.

BasePK: 3033011

Speech:
The hon. member asks who wrote this. I wrote it since the hon. member spoke. It is easy to follow the hon. member, because he tends to repeat the same thing. At the same time, it is only fair to put the facts straight, to let people know what the government has done and what it intends to do, instead of trying to make some drastic change which would not be to the advantage of the people the hon. member represents.

May 10, 1976
The Territories
Since 1967 a number of important changes have been made to the two territorial acts. I will now provide, as a reminder for the benefit of my colleagues, a brief description of what those amendments did to further the constitutional evolution of the two territories.
In June, 1970, amendments to the Yukon Act and Northwest Territories Act were passed by parliament which were in keeping with the recommendations of the Advisory Commission on the Development of Government in the Northwest Territories-the Carrothers Commission-and were designed to increase the local responsibility of the territorial governments and the councils, and to further the federal government's policy of constitutional development in the north.
Speaking on second reading of Bill C-212, an act to amend the Yukon Act, the Northwest Territories Act and the Territorial Lands Act, on May 13, 1970, the previous minister of Indian affairs and northern development, now President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Chretien), described the purpose of the bill in the following way:
... it is aimed at promoting the constitutional development of both territories, in the sense that it will enable their residents to assume more responsibility in the day-to-day administration of their respective governments.
Essentially, because the amendments to both acts were passed, the life of each territorial council was increased from three to four years from the date of the return of the writs for a general election, subject to dissolution by the governor in council at an earlier date in consultation with the respective councils; the commissioners in council were authorized to prescribe the qualifications of persons who may vote or be elected in territorial council elections; the commissioners in council were empowered to legislate on matters concerning the administration of justice in the two territories; the requirements for the commissioners to seek the approval of the governor in council to lend or invest money from the territorial consolidated revenue fund were removed; the period of disallowance of territorial ordinances was reduced from two years to one year; and the commissioners in council were empowered to set the indemnities and allowances of the members of the two councils and the members of council committees.
Additional amendments to the Northwest Territories Act altered the size of the council from 12 to 14 members by increasing the elected membership from seven to ten and reducing the appointed councillors by one, from five to four. There was also a provision authorizing the commissioner in council to further reduce the number of appointed councillors, subject to the approval of the governor in council.
In the same speech on May 13, 1970, the minister further announced a major step to be taken in the constitutional development of the Yukon Territory, although it did not appear in the bill; the establishment of an executive committee. In June, 1970, he instructed Commissioner Smith to establish an executive committee comprising the commissioner, his two assistant commissioners, and two members of the council nominated by the council. The details were discussed by the council at a special session held in June and July. During debate the concept of the executive com-

mittee was endorsed by councillors who recognized its significance as an important step towards the development of an executive along provincial lines.
In 1972 the minister confirmed the government's policy when he announced before the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development that the federal government had adopted seven major objectives for northern Canada. One of those national objectives is "to further the evolution of government in the northern Territories". Although those objectives were stated in general terms, they were "comprehensive in scope and closely related to Canada's national goals and interests," to use the minister's words. Then one year later, in March 1973, the minister again addressed the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development and reported that:
Political development in the Northwest Territories has been one of our greatest concerns since the Carrothers Commission report in 1966 and, as I mentioned in my statement to this committee on March 28, 1972, one of our national objectives in northern development over the next ten years is to "further the evolution of government in both northern Territories". Of course, in this area much has already been achieved, both Territorial Councils are very aggressive in carrying out their responsibilities. Most of the provincial-type government services, with the exception of resource development, are now under the control of the Territorial governments and as in the past, my estimates provide for increased financial assistance to both the Yukon and Northwest Territories Governments.
Mr. Speaker, in light of what I have said before, and with all due respect to my colleague, the hon. member for the Yukon, I do not think the population of the northern territories has been considered as a second-class population, nor can I share the view that the population of the two territories has had to suffer in the past by reason of the so-called colonial status of the Territories. I would think that the hard times and the difficulties of life in the north are the result of climatic, geographic, economic and social circumstances rather than the political or constitutional arrangements. BasePK: 3033065

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, I ask leave under the provisions of Standing Order 43 to present a motion which is of serious urgency to those who are adversely affected by the legislation as it now stands. I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow):
That this House urges the President of the Treasury Board to introduce the necessary amendments so that widows of public servants, of Canadian Armed Forces and RCMP personnel and of others in corresponding categories, will be entitled to the pensions their husbands paid for regardless of the date of marriage, thus ending an instance of discrimination that is most unfair.

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, it is very difficult to try to analyse what is going through the thought processes of each individual labour leader in the country with respect to what the hon. member has asked. All I can say is that I think it should be underlined that labour has withdrawn from these bodies; they have not resigned nor have they quit. It should be pointed out that their withdrawal paves the way for their participation later when they think the time might be appropriate. As to when is the appropriate time, I am afraid that is a question they will decide themselves, and certainly the CLC convention coming up next week will have a part to play in that.

BasePK: 3033313

Speech:
The hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) suggests that usury should be a capital offence, and I am inclined to agree with him.
This is the problem with which we are faced. The step the hon. member suggests is a step in the right direction, but it is a very small step toward solving the problem of high interest rates. I know the hon. member is one who is concerned about people. I have known him for a few years. He is a fellow lawyer and I think he is concerned about people. If we are concerned about people we have to be concerned about their housing problems. We have to build affordable houses, as the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Danson) suggests. If we are to build affordable houses we must look at interest rates. We must have interest rates which give the borrower a fair chance to pay off his mortgage. The only way this can be done is by having low interest rates. It is up to the government to control interest rates with regard to housing so that people can afford them.
It is up to the Minister of State for Urban Affairs to bring forth legislation which controls financial institutions, banks, mortgage companies, trust companies, and insurance companies so they do not charge unconscionable and usurious interest rates.
In order that the bill is not talked out let me conclude by saying I am in favour of it but, my gracious, it is a very short step with respect to a big problem.

Mr. Speaker, I thank hon. members. I will not be long and will deal with but two or three other highlights. As we are talking of industrial strategy, it would be inappropriate not to draw to the attention of Parliament our new competition policy, phase one of which is already being implemented. It goes a long way to ensuring genuine competition in society. Further steps must be taken, but what has been done is particularly important to businessmen. Many people look on competition policy as important to the consumer, which it is; but it is also important to small and medium-sized businessmen: it will make sure they are not put out of business by the large, multinational corporations. The government's policy in this regard is a giant step forward in the right direction in terms of economic strategy. Other steps will be taken when phase two of the competition policy is introduced. These, too, will be found helpful in the area of activity with which we are concerned.
May I mention briefly the new Canadian corporations' legislation which has done much to protect the investors of this country and will encourage our investors to invest in Canadian corporations. The legislation provides the minimum protection needed and will ensure that Canadians may invest with confidence in Canadian enterprises. The legislation has cut out much red tape in the incorporating of federally-incorporated businesses. That will help the businessmen of this country. Perhaps we should go fur-

ther, to remove some of the impediments or some of the negative aspects, let us say, concerning Canadian businessmen. I refer, for example, to the multiplicity of forms to do with UIC, social insurance, and so on, which take up the time of businessmen. I feel that the departments of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, Industry, Trade and Commerce and others should get together and see what can be done to minimize the numbers of forms, etc., which businessmen are required to complete, so that instead of providing this free service to the government our businessmen can spend more time increasing productivity.
The Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce is involved with many programs of research and development which will enhance productivity. I spoke about these at some length a couple of days ago in the House of Commons. Also, we must do what we can to help the businesses of this country compete with international businesses or corporations based in other countries.
Lastly, may I draw the attention of the House to programs of manpower retraining, on-the-job training, and so on, which the federal government instituted in an attempt to match the capabilities of our work force with the requirements of the business community. Such programs are most important. One cannot consider unemployment and industrial strategy without taking into account the necessity of upgrading the skills of our work force and matching those skills with the needs of society.
I thank the House for its indulgence, Mr. Speaker. I wished to say more but will not as I do not wish to abuse the privilege granted to me. I conclude by saying that an industrial strategy we need, and an industrial strategy we have. These authorities and justifications can be used to support arguments on either side of the question, it seems to me.
The House has discussed rehabilitation and the undeniable possibility of miscarriage of justice, of someone being found innocent, after all, after the sentence of capital punishment is carried out.
The argument which has moved me enormously is the one concerning the social implications of capital punishment, the argument that says that if we examine those who have been the victims of capital punishment over the decades we shall find that they are not a cross-section of Canadians, not even a cross-section of criminals in our system. They have been the poor, the people at the bottom of our economic and social system. They, invariably, seemed to be the ones to suffer the penalty of capital punishment.

I suggest that public opinion is an extremely important factor in the determination of an issue like capital punishment. The system of justice in our country after all is the people's system. It must be a system which accords with the population' sense of what is right and fair, and which makes the Canadian people feel secure. Although individual members of parliament perhaps spend more time studying this question than the man in the street, and are exposed to a greater cross-section of argument and expertise, all of which must be brought to bear on our deliberations, when you come right down to it we are asked on behalf of the people of Canada to provide a system of justice they think is fair.
I do not see how any member of this House can escape the undeniable fact that the majority of the people of Canada are of the opinion-however you want to measure

or count it-that there is a place for capital punishment in our system of justice. I insist that this House must respond to that concern.

You cannot hold a referendum on the subject because some people feel you should retain capital punishment for hijacking, treason, and kidnapping; others, that it should be retained in the narrow case of murderers who commit murder for pay. Surely something can be done about this problem. If the restraint program is to be applied to the Post Office, and I do not disagree with that, it should not be applied in a discriminatory way in respect of the development of new services. The people who live in this postal area are entitled to have their mail delivered in the same way it is delivered to other people in the area. I am told that although there are only 24 new households on this walk, the postmen on either side already have a full schedule of households and that under the union agreement neither of them is permitted to add even these extra 24 homes on the street and which are now occupied.
I would think that between a more equitable application of the controls program and some reasonable discussion with the postmen concerned on either side and with their bargaining representatives, it might be possible to return to doing the job which the Post Office is bound to do, which is to deliver the mail to the people living in that area. I hope that the minister will have some good news for us.
I was particularly disturbed-and I will conclude with that-to see him note in the letter that it would be necessary to wait until the limitations or restraints are removed. This restraint program is in effect for three years. Does that mean that the people on Blackhawk Way in north Toronto will have to wait for three years before they can start to get postal delivery? I would remind the minister that the Post Office, to which they have been invited to walk, is over a mile away from some of the houses on that street.
May 21, 1976

Mr. Speaker, on December 3, 1975, I asked the then acting Prime Minister for information on Canada's sales of military equipment. This was but one of many efforts through oral and written questions to learn the facts of this country's extensive dealing in arms.
After being on the order paper for over a year, a question of mine elicited the reply that we sold arms to 73 countries, ranging from A to Z-Abu Dhabi to Zambia. Taiwan bought arms as recently as 1974.
While the minister declared that we did not sell arms of any kind to countries in the Middle East, I found the list included Iran, Israel, Kuwait, Muscat and Oman, Saudi Arabia, Union of Arab Emirates, countries either in or very interested in the Middle East.
In reference to the Middle East one notes in the reply at page 9367 of Hansard for November 24, 1975, that Israel appears on the list for every year from 1963-1974 while the few Arab states noted are much less frequently on the market. One is struck by the fact that none of the so-called confrontation states, Egypt, Jordan or Syria, are shown as having been sold any Canadian military equipment.
In such a sensitive area and in regard to a situation of such delicacy, this seeming discrimination may be serious indeed. This is especially the case in light of the minister's

Adjournment Debate
denial that the government viewed sales of conventional arms as purely business transactions where the dollar value was the only value worth considering. Indeed the ministerial disquisition on arms sales was one of the most fascinating if totally mystifying verbal exercises I have heard in my 19 years in this Chamber. Some of the gems were, "We do have regard to sales of military equipment of all kinds in all directions"; and again: "We also have some categories that might be termed military equipment of a rather innocent character..." The minister also declaimed, "There are certain types of arms and equipment for warlike purposes that we do not supply. Many of the things we supply are not intended for the purpose of killing people." So moved was he that the sedate and normally restrained member for Prince Edward-Hastings (Mr. Hees), could not forbear the comment, "They are 'soft arms' are they?"
But while the response may have had its hilarious aspect, the subject matter is far from amusing. In absolute terms Canada ranks sixth among the world's arms salesmen, exceeded only by the U.S., the U.S.S.R., France, the U.K., and Italy. Among the merchants of death our peace-loving country is by no means in the background. Although Canadians are often accused of lacking aggressiveness in seeking world markets, we are not such shrinking violets when it comes to peddling death-dealing weaponry or related implements of military conflict.
It is very difficult to get a clear picture of what exactly is our role in the field of arms sales. We are told that much must remain secret lest the breach in confidentiality injure the competitiveness of certain Canadian firms. Because of changing formats and departmental reorganization it is not easy to obtain data on the full role of government in the process. The annual report of the Canadian Commercial Corporation is about as quantitatively informative as the average container of breakfast cereal. To those hon. members desirous of information on this very serious matter I would commend the book "Making a Killing" by Ernie Regehr, and the article in Saturday Night, volume 86, 1971, "Dealing Out Death Discreetly; The Traffic in Canadian Arms", by William Cobban.
I believe we must be more realistic and more revealing on this question. I do not think we can on this or any other question have it both ways. We cannot trot out our selfrighteous purity in the nuclear field and then sell arms of another kind to anyone who wishes to buy them, whether they be in the Third World or elsewhere. If we are to adopt the attitude that business is business and who kills whom with Canadian arms is not an issue, then let us say so. But to suggest seriously that Canada sells only gentle, kindly items of military hardware is a bit much even in this age of double talk and slick salesmanship. If our considerations are based on moral judgments and values it does not matter whether we are talking about the nuclear destruction of 100,000 people or the killing of a few hundred so-called political enemies by rifles or machine guns which were in their heyday in the second world war.
In my school days I recall a poem which reflected upon the then sophisticated armaments of the so-called civilized west and their destruction of the peoples of other areas. The author described these machines of mass killing as,
"means of death, and so may be a dagger in a damsel's hand."
I hope we will have an end to the notion that Canada sells not hard but soft, not bad but good military arms. I hope, Sir, that we will have the whole matter examined, and check out the relationship of principles to pocket books.

-a corporation that is ultimately accountable, through a minister, to parliament for the conduct of its affairs.
When a Crown corporation such as Air Canada has a $12,473,000 deficit, an audit and accounting system that has completely broken down, and has the nerve to state they want a fare increase, the Auditor General should move in immediately. A directive should be issued by the government to have an immediate audit conducted. All the contracted work should be returned to the finance branch in Winnipeg. The Auditor General should audit the financial accounts of all Crown corporations whose expenditures directly affect the budgetary accounts of Canada.

The Auditor General should have the right of access to the financial records and documents of all Crown corporations of which he is not the auditor, as he deems necessary to the fulfilment of his responsibilities as auditor of the accounts of Canada.

Our examination included a general review of the accounting procedures and such tests of accounting records and other supporting evidence as we considered necessary in the circumstances.
We are not interested in a general review of Air Canada. We are interested in a complete and proper audit. This document should be questioned as to whether it is worthwhile. I imagine it was very costly, yet all we get out of it is a general review.

June 1, 1976

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, I notice a strange ambivalence on the part of hon. members opposite with regard to unemployment insurance.
June 3, 1976

This plan has always enjoyed, in large measure, the support of members on all sides of the House. It puts into practice the principle that we are our brother's keeper. It gives members of our society while unemployed, and seeking an opportunity to return to the work force, the support they deserve.
As I said in the beginning the business community voiced its concern. Now as of 1976 the difficulties connected with the program are widely recognized far beyond the business community and the present budget is designed to correct those very difficulties which are of concern to members of the community at large. No matter which neighbourhood of my constituency I visit, I hear people grumbling about individuals who are on unemployment insurance and who, in the opinion of neighbours, ought to be working or would be working if a genuine incentive existed to find a job. I occasionally hear parents say this sort of thing about young people.
Let me tell the House something that happened to me not long ago. Last Friday afternoon I received six students from my riding. They attend York University. One of them came up here to work in a government department; the job, starting this summer, is to be permanent. The other five were on unemployment insurance. Well, they had been students for the year and, as it turned out, had all worked last summer. Therefore having worked for eight, nine or 12 weeks last summer, they were qualified for and entitled to unemployment insurance if they could not find a job.
I told them that I had seen help wanted ads in shop windows in the shopping centre where my constituency office is located. There were signs saying, "Cashier Wanted," and "Help Wanted," and so on. I asked these young people if they knew about such opportunities, and had tried to take advantage of them. They said to me, "Well, no. This is how we looked for our jobs-we sent out nearly 100 letters to all sorts of businesses, asking for jobs." They said that none of these letters produced an offer of employment; they felt that, having spent nearly $10 on postage in conducting their job search, they were entitled to claim unemployment insurance. I can imagine how parents who work all their lives feel when confronted with a situation like that. But they tried for a job, continued to write letters, and to claim unemployment insurance.
Let me refer to some statistics which the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras) brought to the fore when he spoke the other day. He said that in a majority of cases those who claimed unemployment insurance for the maximum period after eight to 11 weeks of work were able, when their qualifying period ran out, to find employment. A large percentage found work within six weeks. I think that many of them are like the students who came to my office from my part of the city of Toronto. They may not be aware of where to find work. Or, if they were given a greater incentive to find work, many would be able to do so, I am sure.
I think the changes in the plan will benefit regions like mine. The changes proposed by the government are changes in the right direction. They will increase employment, not increase the number of people on welfare. Not only will they lead to increased employment; they will lead to increased productivity in our economy. There are labour shortages in every sector.
The Budget-Mr. Kaplan
I turn now to the problems we encounter in some depressed regions of the country. There the situation is quite different. I understand that there you cannot go into a shopping centre, as you can in Toronto, and find jobs advertised in store windows. It is hard to find work in those areas. The question we must ask ourselves-and the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie) asked it but without looking at the answers-is this: is unemployment insurance the kind of constructive program which will produce employment in depressed areas of this country, or must we do something else? Instead of institutionalizing employment can we increase productivity in Canada? Shall we continue features which create a sense of entitlement to a pension? In other words, if we do not change the unemployment insurance program will we make Canadians, especially those in the depressed areas, into a nation of pensioners?
By themselves I think unemployment insurance payments are a false solution, a false source of prosperity and stability for the depressed regions of the country. There is a better way. If the hon. member for Hillsborough had listened to the minister, or read his speech, he would know that the government is making solid proposals for job creation, proposals which will bring development to our depressed regions, and programs which ought to be in place in depressed areas in order to create employment. I believe that most Canadians want to work. It is particularly frustrating for the unemployed in the depressed regions of this country because the jobs are not there.
You cannot have a program that is escalating in cost the way this program is and try at the same time to add something new and substantial to the job creation element. When government expenditures just cannot be permitted to grow at their recent historic rate, you have to cut back some programs in order to expand others. In my view nothing can be more rational than to cut back a program like unemployment insurance where the thrust of it is directed toward providing a kind of false alternative to employment, and to try to develop programs that create employment. I very much welcome that. I think you can be a Liberal and welcome that alternative. I very much approve of what the government has done.

In conclusion, if the Canadian labour movement meet with us around the middle of June, and I have indicated they are willing to do this, we can assure them that it is not the government's policy to decrease or cut back on labour's share either of the Gross National Product or national income. If they can be so convinced on the basis of the statistics I have put before the House, and we can show them that under this program, in real terms, workers' wages and salaries have gone up, perhaps they can be convinced that it is indeed the government's policy to protect in real terms the wages of all workers in this country.
If we could so lay a solid basis for co-operation we could set up the sort of mechanisms to which my colleague, the Minister of Finance, referred in the budget-structural mechanisms for consultation. This idea was the highlight of the Quebec manifesto of the CLC. It suggested how labour could participate with the government in the economic and social policy formation which will evolve during the post-control period. It seems to me that that was a most significant position for the Canadian labour movement to adopt. Mr. Speaker, they want to be involved; they want to be consulted; they want assurance that the government will respond, and that there will be an ongoing basis for such consultation. This may mean that in future we shall see less of the element of confrontation, less of the adversary approach in relations between labour and the government of the day.
Considering this program's record of protecting the organized and unorganized workers, I think it can lay the solid base for ensuring that in future labour's share of our income in real terms does not decrease but continues to increase, and that labour will get its share of the rewards of productivity as this country prospers.

Order, please. Representatives of each of the parties have contributed to the point of order with respect to Standing Order 43 raised by the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Blais). I do not think further contributions on the point are required at this time.
It is important to make one or two brief observations. I suggest, initially, that the assessment of Standing Order 43 made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) was correct. The Standing Order has given the Chair difficulty for some time, a difficulty which arose by virtue of the fact that the order paper called for motions under Standing Order 43 to be raised each day after the question period, which meant that there was an open-ended period of time during which members could attempt to introduce such motions.
At the beginning of the present parliament I began to examine very carefully such motions moved pursuant to Standing Order 43. Since the period of time in which they could be introduced was open-ended, it was incumbent on the Chair to exercise diligence in ascertaining whether

they conformed to the rule. A difficulty arose early during the present parliament, in that since such motions are almost exclusively introduced by opposition members, it appeared as if the Chair was constantly interposing itself between opposition members who introduced such motions and the actual bringing of the motions to the floor of the House with unanimous consent. That was an unfortunate appearance which did not make the life of the Speaker of the House easier.
I think in very large measure that was corrected by the rearrangement of our proceedings from which a very strong self-policing feature has evolved in that motions under Standing Order 43 have a limited life each day. If they are spurious on a repetitive basis by either a member or a caucus, surely that will become a self-policing factor because, on a constant basis, they cut into the time for posing questions which is generally regarded as the most important daily device in this House.
Therefore, the self-policing feature has enabled me to take a much more relaxed attitude toward the content of Standing Order 43 motions. However, I do on occasion refuse to put motions which are frivolous or do not seem to have anything to do with the jurisdiction of this House. Beyond that, as long as they relate to a matter of some importance and urgency, whether it even be in the narrow parochial lines of an individual constituency, that is a matter which might be considered.
That is not the end of the difficulty. There is a difficulty on the other side as well. When there is refusal to give unanimous consent to such a motion, there is often the impression that there appears to be some sentiment expressed contrary to the merits of the motion. That is an unfair interpretation, indeed.

As all hon. members know, motions put forward pursuant to Standing Order 43 seek unanimous consent only for the introduction of the motion. If unanimous consent is given, once the motion is introduced it is a debatable motion which becomes the priority order of the day. Therefore, the question is not so much the merits of the motion involved, but whether the House wishes to give its unanimous consent to set aside the business of the day to debate something else. Often, the putting forward of such a motion seems to carry with it the spirit that if only hon. members would give their unanimous consent the motion would pass without debate. That is a great spirit, but all of us know there is no guarantee of procedural equanimity on all sides. Therefore, there is difficulty with interpretation of the rule, regardless of whether it is an opposition member who wishes to put the motion or government members who refuse to set aside orders of the day in order to debate it, or the Chair with regard to interpreting it.

Capital punishment has been debated in this House four times in the last ten years. The issue is not whether we shall execute one, two or three prisoners a year: the issue is how the whole criminal justice system, the Criminal Code,

the administration of that code in our courts, the legal system, police enforcement and prevention systems of the country can best be made to work and protect our society and its values.

Another 10 per cent of murders were committed during the commission of some other crime such as robbery, arson or sexual assault.

I am therefore opposed to the death penalty and so are most of my senior and most experienced colleagues, simply because its continuance prevents the reforms necessary to increase the effectiveness of criminal justice.

I suppose each of us who takes part in this debate is to some extent ruled and governed by, and our logic is oriented around, the experiences we have had in life. I want to speak from the point of view of the family and close friends of the victims of murder, for they are equally victims with the persons who lost their lives because of a crime of violence.
I know, personally, people who have lost a member of their family to a murderer. In the main, the family and the friends are lost to society, sometimes forever. There is no society, group, agency or government which really cares for those who have lost a member of their family to a murderer. Many of these people never make it back into the mainstream of society. They are lost, empty and sad. There is a sadness about them that many of us cannot comprehend. Some become bitter and withdraw from society because in their view there is no justice. The accused is tried, found guilty and sentenced to death, then has his sentence commuted to life, and in a few short years is back on the streets.
In my riding, like some other large urban ridings, there have been murders. I held in my arms a man who lost his wife and an 18-month old son to a murderer. Not only the family and friends of the murdered victim are lost, but many witnesses who gave testimony at the trial live in fear of their lives as well. They fear for their safety because they know that the accused will possibly be out on a weekend pass or on parole in a few years. The date of parole really becomes a focal point in their lives.
I have a neighbour who lives just around the corner from me who regularly writes to me, and I, in turn, write to the Solicitor General, about a murderer who took his daughter's life. He knows that the man who murdered the four women is going to be out-I believe 1978 is the last date I was told. How do you answer these people? How do you console them? How can they pick up their lives and start anew? What possible help can we give them? How can we allay their fears when they express their concern about a murderer who is about to be released on parole? "Has he fulfilled his debt to society," they ask? June 18, 1976

think people should have ground rules; they should know where they stand if they are being asked to invest or if they are invited into a country in order to invest. Recently, at a Commonwealth Parliamentary Conference in New Delhi, this was one of the central questions raised by all the Commonwealth members, because what is becoming quite obvious is that while many of the third world countries resent and find the yoke of the multinationals somewhat difficult, they are so desperate for development that they are willing to have development at almost any cost and under almost any conditions. When we look at prevention we must consider smoking, alcohol, and the provision of drugs, both medical and non-medical, which in my view are abused to a great extent. We must look to the government for leadership in lifestyle modification, changes in habits in terms of advertising and of trying to change public habits and attitudes in those areas which are so thoroughly unhealthy.
The next matter we should consider is nutrition. A dramatic example is the one of the farmers on Parliament Hill, which should make us realize that in a country which overproduces milk to the extent we do now, and where Coca-Cola is sold at approximately the same price, there is something wrong. We can make national provision of milk for school lunches right across the country without any trouble and at minimum cost. In the long run this will lower our medical costs because of the nutritional value of that product, which we should be pushing in our schools rather than pop and other junk foods.
We should encourage all Canadians to continue to have routine medical examinations. The result of this legislation will be the beginning of deterrent fees, a clear backward step from what we have become accustomed to. When we get back to the reasons for the bill, the argument is that costs are rising so fast and are so out of line that we have no choice but to cap them at this end. When you examine the figures, you find that sort of argument questionable indeed. The figures for the increase in medical care costs, the increase in the federal contribution, are quite interesting. When you break them down on a national basis, you find that in 1972-1973 the increase was 7.6 per cent; in 1973-1974 it was 8.8 per cent; and in 1974-1975 it was 6.6 per cent. Each year the increase was well below inflation in Canada, yet here we have a government which does not even want to keep its increasing contribution in step with the rate of inflation. Even that is too much. This is a niggardly, Scrooge approach to the question of the provision of medical care.
It is interesting that in my own province of British Columbia the federal contribution was 13.9 per cent in 1970-1971. It was reduced all the way down to 5.9 per cent in 1974-1975, and 1974-1975 was the year of the NDP government in that province which allegedly was squandering money; at least this was the theory abroad. It is certainly not indicated in the provision of medical care in that province or the reduction of the federal government's contribution to those medical services. As I say, the capping is unnecessary. The costs are not increasing at a rate which is inordinate or unreasonable, and by limiting the increase we are taking away the provincial inducement to move into new areas.
One area with which I want to deal now and which I think is most important is environmental health. More and more in this country we find that as we alter the natural state of the environment, as we provide new chemicals and new pesticides, and as we provide insulating materials such as asbestos and new plastics, new forms of cancer emerge. We cannot let that happen to the Canadian people. But by abandoning the federal contribution in medicare

that is exactly what we are doing. The standard of living that we have in this country in the south is now becoming dependent upon the poisoning of Indians in the north.
It is to our shame that we see at English river, in northwestern Quebec, in Mistassini and other places, our native people suffering from Minamatas disease. The reason they have been suffering from Minamata disease is that the standard of life in the south is higher. We have industrialized areas in the north and we have taken risks with the future of the Indians. What are we repaying them with? The most we are doing at English River is to tell them not to eat the fish.
It is time we did something in terms of full compensation for native people but, most important, it is time we learned a lesson from Minamata disease in this country, that you do not move into an area in a rush for spoils, profit and money in the process of which you destroy the environment and kill the native people. That has been the tradition in this country. Let us make no mistake about it. We have nothing to be proud of in the way we settled Canada, in terms of our native population. That is what we are still doing when we consider the mercury poisoning that is now taking place in these areas of Canada.
We have a real problem with vinyl chlorides in the provision of plastics. Liver cancers are developing at an alarming rate. The interesting thing about preventing cancer is that it takes 20 years for lung cancer to develop in asbestos workers. The workers themselves do not feel the immediate risk, although they are running a high risk daily. They need the money, they have to continue to work. We cannot sit idly by as parliamentarians, nor can this government sit idly by and let this continue. We still do not have mandatory regulations regarding the use of masks in asbestos mines. Admittedly, we brought in some ambient air standards.
We still have not done anything with regard to tailings or with regard to drill standards. The wind can blow tailings all over the place. Only a minor amount of asbestos causes cancer. Are we to abandon the fight against cancer because of this government's niggardly approach to medical care and its tragic departure from principles in which they once believed? There is no question that what we are seeing in Bill C-68 is the end of the purported just society and the end of those great promises of 1968. It is all over now.

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, we are thankful to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) for the statement he made in the House today on the serious problem of the strike in air transport. We deplore that such a strike has happened. However we doubt that the commission will be able to proceed quickly enough to allow us to take the necessary procedures so that the problem will not drag on for days and weeks. We are now waiting for the commission's report and, during that time, the Canadian economy is unfortunately burdened with serious problems because air transport in Canada today has become very important, and we know it.
Mr. Speaker, some individuals make it a specialty to turn this problem into a racial issue under the guise of safety. In the last paragraph, the minister said in French, and I quote:
Experience in recent years has shown that while making for better comprehension bilingualism can increase the safety of operations.
I do not think the minister included this sentence in his statement without checking its meaning. Bilingualism can increase air safety. When we see individuals now making a pretext of safety for disrupting air transport, particularly in Quebec, I think that unfortunately they are using a false pretext to cover up a racial issue. We know very well that studies have been made and that in certain other countries more than one language are used even in communications and other areas, and that nowhere else as far as we know has there been a strike because of the hazards the language used in those other countries would have caused.
Mr. Speaker, I myself had the opportunity in recent days when several of my colleagues were caught in the middle of this air strike and remained grounded because air services were no longer working, I had the opportunity to meet a unilingual anglophone, a pilot who feels that this safety issue is a false problem in air transport. He does not believe a word of it. Yet he does not speak French and he is a pilot from western Canada who believes they are creating a problem from a false situation. We wish, therefore, that a solution can be reached by the federal government, which should make it possible for Canada to remain a bilingual country. As far as I know, we still are in Canada, we have two official languages and we should not allow some individuals, under false arguments or for other pretexts, to take steps which will result in one of the official languages of Canada not being recognized in a public service as important as Air Canada or air transport in general. We therefore support the means-not radical means, but means of understanding, we hope-to be taken by the federal government to have the French language respected in Quebec, because it is the official language of Quebecers and one of the country's official languages. We must have the French language respected and prove wrong those who take pleasure in repeating that under the cover of safety, we must use only the English language, and particularly in Quebec.

Another federal policy with implication for Alberta hog producers is the domestic feed grain policy. We announced some changes in this policy three weeks ago.

Canadian Wheat Board Act (No. 2) agency. If it is going to serve its purpose in the best interests of the producer, those people who are commissioners and those who are members of the advisory committee must have complete freedom.
I really have no quarrel with western grain filling the requirements of the eastern feeder-not at all. I realize and recognize the value of the feeding industry in Canada; nevertheless I have a concern that the advisory committee of the Canadian Wheat Board as well as the commissioners could hamstring this policy which has been announced by the Minister of Agriculture and the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board because it is tied to corn. The price of western grain is tied to corn f.o.b. Montreal.
I have no quarrel whatsoever with the element of competition, but if eastern feeders can buy United States corn from Chicago cheaper than they can buy western grain-at less money than the western producer can get if he ships it to the west coast or through the port of Churchill-I have to question the economics of it. It is not taking anything away from the eastern feeder as long as his requirements are met, but I do not see why we should throw money down the drain to fill a market that could adequately be filled from some other source.
I am sure the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board recognizes that you can put corn on the Montreal market cheaper and with less freight involved than that which comes from western Canada. It takes $11 a ton to move it from Thunder Bay to Montreal, but only $9 a ton from Toledo to Montreal, and that adds up to a lot of money.

Mr. Speaker, my remarks tonight on the capital gains tax on farm property are based on the questions I asked the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) on June 17 as recorded at page 14611 of Hansard of that date. The first question
was:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. It relates to the capital gains tax on family farm property. A family farm operator, during his lifetime, directs all his profit to the improvement of his farm and equipment. When the farm is sold upon his retirement, the proceeds become his sole private pension fund. It is therefore grossly unfair to use capital gains tax to seriously reduce this pension. Will the minister consider amending the Income Tax Act to permit a once-in-a-lifetime sale of a family farm without attracting capital gains tax?
The minister's reply was simply this:
Well, Mr. Speaker, there are certain provisions now with regard to family farms but I do not see at this time the opportunity to be able to expand those.
The second question was a supplementary and along a similar line. It was as follows:
Mr. Speaker, since the capital gains taxes collected on family farm property amount to only 10 per cent of the total collected on property generally, would the minister weigh the appraisal and accounting costs, plus the major irritant effect of this tax, against the net revenue derived and hopefully remove this unfair and unjust tax altogether?
June 28, 1976

I felt that the minister's response was altogether too brief. He simply said:
... it of course has to be relevant also to the question of equity to other taxpayers.
I suggest that the answers were entirely unsatisfactory in the light of the importance of capital gains taxes and the way they affect farmers, particular family farmers, and also small businessmen.
The reason for this particular question relates to activity going on in the riding I represent, Norfolk-Haldimand. There has been expropriation or threat of expropriation of a very large section of farmland. This is to serve as the industrial sites for hydro, Stelco and Texaco, and also for the satellite city which is to be built in that area. The province has just completed a land assembly program there. This, of course, resulted in the forced sale of many farms. I think there has never been such a concentration of farmers paying capital gains tax in such a small area as the one I just described.
The farmers whose properties have been sold in the manner I described are having income tax returns reassessed, and a whopping capital gains tax is being imposed upon them. Tax paid, of course, is on one half of the capital gain derived from the valuation day value subtracted from the value at the time of the sale. The government land appraisers have assigned abnormally and unrealistically low valuation day values of something in the neighbourhood of $350 to $400 per acre. The sale value has been in the neighbourhood of $2,000 plus per acre. Therefore the capital gain is $1,600, and the tax on half of that is a tax on $800 per acre. On a 100 acre farm that is a capital gains tax assessed on an amount of $80,000, which is certainly drastic and exorbitant.
A $400 valuation day value is totally unrealistic. The government appraisers are not in touch with reality, and one wonders if any of them have ever operated a family farm.
The farmers are angry. They are pooling their resources to fight the assessment of capital gains in the manner described. They are going through the formal appeal procedures as laid down in the act. They are going through the courts, and if necessary, they will even go to the highest court in the land to see that justice is done.
The minister is aware of this situation because of previous letters from me to him on this matter, and I feel it is time to face up to this giant rip off which is being perpetrated against the farming community in Norfolk-Haldi-mand.
Let us examine the effects of this unconscionable action. As I said in my question, it destroys farmers' retirement funds. During his lifetime a farmer puts his profits back into improving his farm, his buildings, and his equipment. The value increases. Upon retirement he sells the farm. The proceeds become his pension fund; he has no other.
The bandits from National Revenue pounce upon this fund and wipe out this one opportunity to retire with dignity. The farmers have pride. In my opinion they are the last bastions of independence and free enterprise. The tradition of providing for their own retirement goes back for generations.

Mr. Speaker, allow me to make one or two very simple points. First of all, in support of the House leaders of the other parties in their statements that this was a proposal put forward as a result of discussion among the House leaders, it was not specifically a government proposal but it was one put forward on behalf of all the House leaders who felt, as I did, that it would be undesirable to have snap votes without notice on a measure which is not a government bill in the ordinary sense because no question of confidence is involved.
The views of members are being sought as individuals, not as members of parliament, and that is why this sort of provision is being made, just as it was on second reading. It would, of course, be possible that any of the amendments at the report stage could change the whole nature of the proposal which is being debated in the House, so the voting at the report stage is almost as crucial as the vote on third reading. That is why we have had to include report stage amendments as well as the vote on third reading. We considered this matter at some length, and the conclusion we reached is one which is, in my view, irrefutable.
May I say, in response to the hon. member for Crowfoot, that as far as I know I have not been party to a proposal of this kind in relation to an ordinary government bill. This is a special procedure which relates to a measure which is of a different character, one in which each member has an equal interest. It is not a question of partisan support or party loyalty, but a matter of individual conscience, and for this reason I hope the House will support the motion.

(1) A committee-

It seems to me that at least an equal amount of violence will replace that which the minister and the government are trying to prevent. Until our system of justice, including rehabilitation and parole, becomes more refined and realistic, I cannot justify in my mind the total abolition of capital punishment.

July 6, 1976

under the kind of control that would justify the vast majority of the people of Canada having confidence that their rights will be preserved and their protection improved by removing the death penalty. On the contrary, I think a vast number of people in this country feel a sense of betrayal on the part of the government in failing to provide protection for them in general, and for policemen and prison guards in particular.
I agree with all those who say that members of parliament must reflect their own consciences. Nevertheless I think it is incumbent on the government to recognize that perhaps as high a percentage of Canadians as 80 per cent feel very uneasy about the removal of the death penalty. In taking this extraordinary step surely the government should be able to point to some sort of improvement in prison conditions and in the administration of justice that will replace the security that many people feel the death penalty represents. Otherwise this would not be such an issue and you would not have eight out of 10 Canadians writing in to protest the death penalty being taken away.
If hon. members support this motion they will surely be coming to grips with the basic proposition that, in allowing police and prison guards to risk their lives to protect the rights and properties of Canadians, police and prison guards ought to have, as I maintain all Canadians ought to have, some sort of specialized protection. I want to speak now for a few moments of other changes I have seen, some of which I am happy with, and some of which make me less happy.
One of the changes that I have seen over the last 25 years is the rapid urbanization of our country. I realize that this urbanization is not necessarily due to the vital growth of urban centres but also represents, on the other side of the scale, a hemorrhage of the life's blood of the small towns in rural Canada.
I regret that our development as a country has been so uneven. Over the last 25 years there has been a lusty but sometimes malignant growth of our urban centres, especially of areas based on the rapid exploitation of non-renewable resources. It is obvious, of course, that a civilization, a culture, or an economy based on non-renewable resources is, by definition, non-renewable itself. I regret the prodigal squandering of our natural resources which should be the precious capital of a civilization as long as it lasts, for a continuing civilization and culture must be based on renewable resources to be renewable themselves.
Of course I am probably biased in this matter because by birth and a long life of experience I am a country man, vividly
October 18, 1976

aware of the fact that we as humans are part of the web of life and that, if we forget that fact, we forget it at our peril.
I believe that this uneven development of our country is not entirely unavoidable or inevitable. Much of it has been caused by bias, often unconscious bias, in the whole apparatus of government at every level, based on the false premise that was instilled perhaps 40 or 50 years ago but which is no longer valid, namely, that the good life can be obtained only in an urban setting. Experience has proved the opposite to be true.
There was a time some decades ago when modern conveniences, modern communications and so on, were the prerogatives of the urban area, but that is no longer true. Technology has advanced to the point where those who live in rural Canada can enjoy all the modern conveniences, if they can afford them, that the urban dweller can, and have the joy and benefit and recreational facilities-and I mean recreational in the best sense of the word-and the experience, of living in the country. I believe that the highest and best quality of life is achievable more easily in rural Canada and in the small towns than it is in the large urban centres.
I do not think it is inevitable that modern technology forces us to the large urban conglomeration of society. This has come about, I think, because of a worship of giantism and an over selling of the benefits of large scale. It is known that in similar situations along the Trent when water levels were lowered for construction purposes, fish and aquatic mammals were killed and nearby wells have gone dry. The uplift of ice when spring freshet commences is often more severe with lower river levels and usually there is more damage caused to docks and bank protection. Officials have calculated that the amount of storage provided by such a lowering would have delayed the high water levels in 1976 by about a half day but would not have reduced the maximum levels reached.
The minister has asked that the petition be studied in detail. Game and fish authorities have already been asked to give their advice. An opinion has also been requested from an independent engineering firm as to what effect an all winter lowering would have on ice build-up. The clearing of ice jams in the Ottawa area is a municipal operation assisted by canal procedures to flush away the broken ice. Similar co-operation would be given the upstream municipalities if they wished to provide a similar service on a co-ordinated basis.
The control of water in a watershed has many ramifications besides maintaining levels for navigation. They have an effect on the water level in wells, fish and marine life, and the quality of the water itself. Departmental officials are constantly trying to improve the art to accommodate as many users as possible with minimum adverse effects. Precipitous action might have unexpected and undesirable results. It is for this reason that this complex problem requires detailed multi-disciplinary study.

Speech:
For some years it has been the position of my party that not only should there be two separate ministers fulfilling these responsibilities, but that there should be two departments, distinct and separate, one for fisheries, and one for the environment. We repeat that position. We see no reason at all to change our position in this regard. We made our views known some years ago and events since then have only reinforced our belief, namely, that this is a proper and justifiable position.
It is apparent to us that the government is either unaware of the basic difference of these two departments or, in the alternative, is so completely indifferent to their individual importance that it chooses to reject the national and international implications connected with the operations of these two units of the government.
Surely one need not be an expert to appreciate that the nature of Fisheries is economic, social, and even cultural. On the other hand, one does not need great perceptual insight to appreciate that with respect to the environment we are dealing basically with scientific research. By their very nature, activities concerning Fisheries and the environment should be distinct and separate from each other. In ignoring this fact the government has undoubtedly weakened both sectors, at a time, unhappily, when both should have been strengthened.
One might say that combining these two activities under one minister is justiFied in terms of restraint. If the government had so ordered its economic priorities as to indicate some justiFication for this uniFication of function that would have been fine. But those priorities have not been made known; they have not been forthcoming. It seems to me that, in the absence of such justification, and having regard to the size of the present cabinet, such alleged restriction in government spending can only be an excuse for this combination, not a reason. Only the government's unwillingness to embark on progressive action and to undertake its responsibilities in the Fields of fisheries and the environment has led it along this course.
If I have time I shall return to this topic and deal with the very structure of the department. At the moment I want to deal with what the Speech from the Throne had to say about the environment. I suppose hon. members opposite would be only too happy if I said absolutely nothing about the topic, because that is exactly what the Speech from the Throne said-nothing. It said absolutely nothing about the environment. We heard of the necessity to place further emphasis on research and development of renewable energy resources, but nothing about measures to regulate exploration and development on federal lands. Again, no mention whatsoever was made of environmental concerns. Yes, we did hear about native peoples' land claims in the James Bay region, but nothing about environmental concerns in that important region. We even heard about our international responsibilities in terms of environmental protection, but nothing about our national responsibilities-and all this from a government which has professed over the years to be concerned about our environment.
In the throne speech of September, 1968, the government talked about the broad importance of the problem of pollution. In October, 1969, in his speech following the throne speech of that year, the Prime Minister spoke about the increasing concern with regard to the environment, about the ruthless destruction of a landscape and the useless pollution of air and water. He spoke of determination to overcome noise, noxious fumes, and the pollution from industrial waste, and said:
First of all, we will never sacrifice, in the name of progress, a clean and healthy environment to industrial or commercial development.
The year 1970 was a vintage year for the environment. The Speech from the Throne had this to say:
Pollution is a many-headed hydra and requires action in many forms. You will be asked to consider bills intended to deal with pollution in two of its aspects: in the ocean and in the atmosphere. More pressing than any single step or steps, however, is the need to co-ordinate and consolidate our efforts in an effective fashion. There will be proposed the establishment of a department to be concerned with the environment and the husbanding of those renewable resources that are a part of and dependent upon it.
This was welcome news for the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Stanfield) who then was leader of the opposition.
The then minister of fisheries was absolutely glowing on October 15, 1970, when he said:
Mr. Speaker, I want to say a few words this afternoon about the establishment of a new Department of Environmental Affairs, and I should like to say at the outset that shaping our Canadian environment is the biggest challenge we face in the 1970's. It is a bigger challenge than unemployment. It is a bigger challenge than inflation. It is a bigger issue than pensions or skyjacking or the FLQ. To many Canadians it is a bigger challenge than all of our financial and social problems put together.
It was the first minister of the environment who said that exactly six years ago last week. Since then it has been all downhill. In 1972 there was just passing reference made. In
1973	there was one brief reference in the throne speech. In
1974	the only reference was a wish to enhance the environment of cities and towns. In September, 1974, there was an almost seeming obsession with the environment. We had an overwhelming two sentences in the throne speech devoted to this subject.
If we need to look for any further evidence of the government's disinterest in the Department of the Environment we have only to realize that there have been four ministers in 24 months. Nothing in this government changes more than ministers of the environment, except economic policy. Therefore one can hardly be surprised at the lack of policy direction which results from this constant changing at the ministerial level. [...truncated]

Thank you, Mr. Speaker; I appreciate the courtesy shown by the House. I did not realize my time was up, but I shall conclude very quickly. In the unified family courts, procedures would be aimed at reconciliation and rehabilitation. I discussed this matter with my provincial counterparts at the conference of attorneys general in Vancouver in June which I hosted. Perhaps I might quote from the communique issued by that conference:
Ministers agreed that priority should be given to the development of unified family courts with broad jurisdiction over all legal matters respecting the family unit.
There was some disagreement over the level at which such courts should be sited, but I am confident that this issue can be satisfactorily resolved and that we can get on with the business of reform in these particular courts which touch so many Canadians. I will be meeting, in the coming months, with ministers of the provinces in an effort to establish, where appropriate, unified family courts. Indeed, negotiations in this direction are already well under way in several provinces and I am confident that progress can be made such as was indicated by the attorney general for Ontario the other day in forecasting possible legislation in that province.
The Law Reform Commission also stressed that there are three economic functions to marriage, wage earning, home care and child rearing, and that the present law on matrimonial property really recognizes only the first, which is usually the contribution of the husband or the wage earning provision and does not recognize the two economic functions which are usually the woman's contribution of home care and child rearing. The commission recommended that the law should provide for the equal sharing of property acquired through the earnings of either or both spouses during the marriage. There would be some exceptions relating to gifts, inheritances, bequests or trusts. The recommendation affecting matrimonial property are of immeasurable importance to married women in Canada. It takes direct aim at the anachronism which exists in the law of most provinces and which was highlighted by the

Supreme Court of Canada in its decision in the now famous case of Murdoch v. Murdoch.
Our ministerial discussions in Vancouver, in June, touched upon this particular subject, and at that time provincial attorneys general expressed the view that matrimonial property is exclusively a provincial matter. This is not a unanimous view. Obviously, the Law Reform Commission had different experts and different views on the federal role involved relating to matrimonial property. The conference did indicate the ministers agreed that provincial governments would be urged to press forward with reform of matrimonial property laws reflecting the concept of marriage as a partnership of equals. I understand, again from press reports, that the attorney general of Ontario plans to table some proposals in this regard very shortly.
I welcome such initiatives to be taken by the provinces and will continue to consult with them to that end. I would point out, however, that if it is their exclusive jurisdiction, they have a responsibility to act, and to act expeditiously. If the provinces do not move expeditiously to put in place meaningful changes in the law relating to matrimonial property to take account of the economic needs and the rights of both spouses, there will obviously be increasing pressure on this parliament to endeavour to try to implement the recommendations, in one form or another, of the Law Reform Commission's report relating to the disposal of matrimonial property. Canadian women should not have to wait much longer for provincial action in this regard. I hope that provincial attorneys general will take note of my remarks, that if it is their jurisdiction, as claimed by them, they should act expeditiously in this area.
We will go forward in the immediate future on three aspects relating to family law. The first is negotiations with the provinces toward the establishment in the provinces of unified family courts. The second is changes in the law relating to matrimonial property to better take account of the economic needs and rights of both parties. The third is formal consultation with those in the community across Canada regarding the other recommendations of the Law Reform Commission's report on family law.
I appreciate the courtesy of the House in allowing me to complete my speech. This is the last day of the debate on the address in reply to the Speech from the Throne. In the Speech from the Throne the government put forward a comprehensive and coordinated program for action by parliament and the country, The object of the debate within the time allotted in our rules gives the opposition a chance to show their disagreement with those proposals and to show that they deserve the confidence of the House. I have read the motions of confidence with great care, as well as the speeches from the opposition. More than 50 per cent of the salary and wage earners in Canada are employed by small businesses. If all small businesses in Canada closed their doors at the same time, the economy would come to a standstill. Large corporations and their workers are protected from the vagaries of market conditions, bureaucratic harassment, cash supply, and other matters. The unionized workers are protected by their unions, and by our labour laws. The large corporations have batteries of lawyers to run interference for them, but not so the small businessman and his workers.
Big business has assets and productive capacity to use as collateral for loans. Small businesses very often have to borrow on faith, and there is never enough of this faith to go around. In the United States they have the small business administration to make loans to small businesses, and also to advise and train people in small business or who want to start up a small business. We need something like that in Canada. There is too much disparity between lending institutions, and between regions, with respect to the availability of small businesses to obtain loans for operating expenses, and to finance expansion.
Without a set government program of loan assistance or guarantee, lending institutions in Canada would rather lend large sums of capital to large corporations, against secure collateral, than to lend small sums to small businesses which often cannot offer blue ribbon collateral. In my view we must recognize that there is another kind of blue ribbon collateral; the initiative, resourcefulness, and determination of the small business entrepreneur in Canada. If we support the people who are presently providing the largest percentage of jobs in our country today, then they will be able to create still more jobs. This would be better than trying to solve the problem by paying out still more unemployment insurance, grants, welfare, and all the other government stop gap measures.
A large percentage of the chronically unemployed in Canada do not have the specialized skills and talents required by most of the large corporations. Small businesses do not require these specialized skills and rare technical talents for the most part.
