Mr. Speaker, my remarks in this adjournment debate this evening are in response to my question to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) on October 15 relating to offshore imports of beef from Australia and New Zealand. I was deeply concerned that although the minister had announced his individual permit requirements before any beef imports would be permitted into Canada-that was after October 17-he had not indicated that he intended to use this device actually to restrict beef imports.
Later on October 19 the joint statement of the Department of Agriculture and Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce did announce Canadian beef import quotas of 17.5 million pounds to apply to all countries importing into Canada as from October 18 to the end of the year, and notably to Australia, New Zealand and the United States.
I acknowledge that this long delayed action will limit beef imports for the remaining two months of this year. But surely as every cattleman in Canada knows, the damage already has been done. The fact remains clear that until this announcement of October 19 Canada was the only country in the world to permit unrestricted access to our beef markets.
In spite of our small human population Canada now ranks as the fourth largest importer of beef in the world. Actually in 1976 Canada is first on the basis of per capita consumption. This is the situation even in the face of our record high domestic production of cattle and beef, especially steers and cows. In spite of the repeated statements by the Minister of Agriculture that these offshore beef imports did not depress our own domestic beef and cattle markets, there is ample evidence to show this is not true and that these massive beef imports, starting after August 12, 1975, have seriously depressed and continue to depress our fed cattle markets and our cow and feeder markets.
In June, 1974, the Montreal Beef Wholesalers Association made available data that clearly support this statement. In addition a comparison of price spreads in Canada and the U.S.A., between hind and front quarters and between all grades of cows, shows up this depressing element in Canada which of course is directly related to the price discounts permitted by Canada on these offshore imports compared to the same imports into the U.S.A. If more evidence is needed on this issue there is an economic paper by Freebairn and Rausser in the November, 1975, issue of the "American

November 1, 1976

Journal of Agricultural Economics" dealing directly with price changes due to beef imports.
There can be no doubt now, three weeks after the U.S.A. triggered its meat import law, that Canada's level of beef exports was the final action that brought on President Ford's October 9 action to control the level of imports into his country. That action was reflected in every cattle and beef market in Canada. Even at Walsh on that same day, which is in my market area, where we had 1,500 feeder yearlings, including my own, there was a drop of about $2 per hundred weight in response to this U.S. action.
Widespread concern by all Canadian cattle producers is now most apparent. Public meetings are being held in every cattle producing region. Very little advance publicity is necessary to get a crowd of cattlemen to discuss this cattle crisis. Three weeks ago in Lethbridge 300 feeders and cow-calf operators turned out with only two days' notice to let off steam, if you like, and draft an appropriate resolution to the minister. 1 was there and spoke to them. Then on October 22 in Stettler 800 concerned cattlemen held another somewhat similar meeting. The Minister of Agriculture will be hearing more about that.
Perhaps the most unique evidence of this national cattlemen's concern is the class action legal suit brought by three Maple Creek, Saskatchewan, ranchers for $52 million against the Minister of Agriculture for failing to take adequate action to curtail Oceanic beef imports. That represents $1 million a .week for a 12-month period which, in their opinion, represents only a nominal loss to the Canadian beef producers. This class action suit is for real and has been properly served by lawyers acting for the Maple Creek ranchers on behalf of all Canadian cattlemen. Those of us who are old enough to remember Canada's flourishing sheep industry under range conditions, especially in western Canada, cannot help but speculate somewhat fearfully that Canada's cattle industry could go down the drain with another big push from these Australian and New Zealand imports, just as was the case in respect of lamb, mutton and wool imports from the same countries 30 years ago.
The answer, of course, is some specific policy direction to control offshore imports to reasonable historical levels and to establish further fair bilateral trade policies in beef and cattle with the U.S.A. I do not mean a supply-management policy promoted by the Minister of Agriculture. His description of the U.S. cattle industry as supply-management oriented because of its meat import law with power to impose import quotas is sheer nonsense.

The preparation of a voters' list is one of the most important stages in a general election. To adequately answer the question as to which system has the least drawbacks and most advantages, we should look at this problem within the framework of some criteria. The first and foremost criterion is the inclusion of the greatest number of names of eligible voters and, conversely, of the least possible number of eneligible voters. The second criterion is the relative cost of preparing the list of voters.
My bill, Mr. Speaker, calls for a continuous, permanent list in which the initiative for registration should lie with the individual. This is not to say that the Crown should not exercise some influence. What we would have is a combination of systems placing the primary responsibility on the voters to register themselves, and also introducing a considerable measure of follow-up action and publicity by election officials to ensure that the greatest possible number of voters do in fact exercise their right. Perhaps the two countries which best illustrate the use of the permanent voters' list are Australia and New Zealand. There is also West Germany. In Australia, however, there is the additional factor of a penalty for those who fail to vote. Indeed before the last Australian general election the Governor General saw fit to remove the prime minister from office. He then dissolved parliament and called another election.
In Australia the permanent voters' list is revised at a specific time-it is like bringing in your car to be tuned; voters get tuned at certain times of the year. In the instance I have cited the election came six months too soon and, as a result, many Australians were disfranchised. This points out the weakness of the system, Mr. Speaker; to be effective it should be kept up almost on a monthly basis.
One of the most ideal countries in the world for the operation of a permanent voters' list would be the United States. It is ironic that we should be discussing this today when they are in the throes of an election. Every four years in the United States there is a presidential election. Even if a president should die during his term, or be removed from office, the vice president carries on until the term expires. It happens quite frequently in that country that the elected President and the Senate and House of Representatives are of the opposite parties. I think

the last time the president was of the same party as the house was during President Johnson's term. The United States is one of the few countries in the world that could use a permanent voters' list on a federal basis. It has been mentioned already that Canada tried this system in July, 1934. But in the 1935 election very few people came out to vote, using the normal procedures. In the end many of the members who were elected on that occasion had to go out and find the people and get them registered because there was no proper system. As the hon. member for St. Catharines (Mr. Parent) pointed out, the arrangement had to be abandoned.

As the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond-Delta (Mr. Reynolds) suggested, by reducing the election period from 60 days to 47 days, $2 million could be saved. But here we are playing around with $4 million to $6 million for a permanent voters list.
It is also likely that an additional 1,200 to 1,300 civil servants would be required to keep a permanent voters list up to date. If we want to hold costs down we must think of these things.
The hon. member for Hochelaga (Mr. Lavoie) referred to the problem of people being missed by enumerators. A permanent voters list would correct that problem.

Actually, statutes passed by the provinces, particularly by Ontario and Alberta, have covered most of this ground for 20 years. Those provincial laws are still adequate.

BasePK: 3056256

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member can make a speech if he wishes. Perhaps he will allow me the courtesy of finishing my speech. The fact is that we have had three different ministers of industry, trade and commerce since 1973. As I said, it is difficult to understand a new portfolio in less than a year, and we have had three ministers appointed in the last three years. I suggest that those ministers did not have time to discover the location of the washrooms in the department. Therefore, how can one expect them to draw up a proper trade policy on the basis of which Canada should negotiate at Geneva?
Let me refer again to the conditions which form the framework for the current round of negotiations in Geneva. The world has changed substantially since the Kennedy Round of negotiations to which I referred. We must now deal with at least three economic blocs. There is the United States block; the European Common Market, which for the first time is negotiating on behalf of all countries forming part of that market, as opposed to having each one of them take its own individual, nationalistic approach; and a third big bloc, the Soviet Union and eastern bloc countries. Japan may herald the emergence of a fourth bloc, and the OPEC nations a fifth bloc. Canada seems to be the odd country, outside of a bloc. The government must explain the reason for this. Is this what it wants? Does it want Canada to be among the few countries in
Canadian Trade Policy
the world isolated from one of the big five economic blocs which have been formed or are in the process of formation, or does it want Canada to join a bloc? In any event, we have the right to know what the government intends in this regard.
Surely the government would wish to present a bipartite policy when engaging in international trade negotiations. Hopefully, it might even consider a tripartite policy which ought to be presented to parliament when engaging in international negotiations. But the government has not done this. Instead, it has engaged in a highly partisan approach; it has dealt in secret and come back to parliament asking for rubber-stamp approval with respect to agreements entered into. Surely the best forum for consultation with respect to trade matters is parliament, the institution of which we are one part. In parliament, the people of Canada, through their elected representatives, have the opportunity to participate in decisions of the day; and, Mr. Speaker, no more important decisions than those currently being taken in Geneva will be made during the balance of this decade.
Let me now turn to tariffs. It is interesting to note the magnitude of the revenues the government derives from certain tariffs. In the 1976 fiscal year, the total revenue was $1,887 million. If we look at the American trade act, it calls for a 100 per cent reduction of tariffs of 5 per cent or less, and a 60 per cent reduction of all other tariffs. If that is the view that prevails in Geneva, and if there is such a cutback in tariffs, it will mean, for example, an estimated $1.1 billion of lost revenue as far as our Customs tariffs are concerned. The odd point is that that fact is not even known by the negotiators who are presently negotiating on our behalf in Geneva.
Often, when we speak in terms of tariffs on trade, we do so in the abstract. However, let us not forget that what we are really talking about is jobs-jobs for Canadians in the electronics industry, the textile field, the leather industry, the furniture industry, the china industry, lock-making and many other diverse forms of activity. That is why we believe, in proposing this motion today, it is urgent that there be a less secretive approach to what is transpiring in parliament, and certainly with regard to our trade negotiations at the present time in Geneva.
It is not just a question of tariffs. Perhaps the most important items that are going to be negotiated in Geneva are the non-tariff items, the so-called subsidies, the countervailing duties. That is where Canadian businessmen, people in the export field and consumers could have an important input in contributing to the negotiations in Geneva, if they were allowed that privilege by this government that is now, temporarily, in office.

BasePK: 3056667

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to raise a point of order. It is an urgent matter and I hope Your Honour will give me the floor for a few moments to develop it.

November 10, 1976
Privilege-Mr. Lang
The House is about to be presented with hundreds of millions of dollars of supplementary estimates. I directed a line of questioning, as did my colleagues today, to the President of the Treasury Board. In my second question I asked if the minister was prepared, as an interim measure, to recommend to his colleagues that at least one department be brought back into the House for examination by committee of the whole, without limitation under Standing Order 58, which is the guillotine rule. I was careful to preface my question by saying that notwithstanding the work of the Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization, which is now seized with drafting a report to the House on rule changes, I would nevertheless go ahead with my question based upon what I consider to be the urgency of the matter, which is the presentation of the estimates to the House, and the evidence given by the Auditor General and his department with regard to the fact that the House and parliament as a whole have lost control over government spending.
I wanted the minister to take leadership and recommend this to his colleagues since he has responsibility to parliament for government spending as President of the Treasury Board, and to recommend on a trial basis that the estimates be brought back into committee of the whole.
I raise this matter because we are all concerned that since the rule changes we have unwittingly become a rubber stamp for government spending. The word is out that parliament has lost control over government spending, and this is a serious matter. Since the new rules came into effect in 1968 government spending has increased by over 300 per cent, yet we as a parliament have no control. The minister should take some initiative in this regard. I know he shares the same concern, as does the Auditor General and as does the Public Accounts Committee. My question to him was merely to suggest that perhaps the supplementary estimates and the main estimates for this year could be brought back into the House since it is evident that the Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization will not act upon this unless there is some direction from the government. I should like to hear from the minister on this.

BasePK: 3056681

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, may I say that it is unfortunate that, on the one day of the year when we remember our war dead and duty, the ceremony in Canada could not take more precedence. I am privileged on behalf of my party to reply to the statement of the Acting Minister of Veterans Affairs on this day, a few hours before the touching Armistice ceremony which will take place at Canada's National Memorial here in Ottawa. We, on my side of the House, endorse fully the statement of the acting minister. We also pay tribute to the Canadian Legion and to all veterans' organizations across this great land who hold dear the true meaning of remembrance as we all remember our fallen comrades on Armistice Day. While we pay tribute to the fallen, we must remember our duty to those who remain.
It is probably difficult to imagine that in 1976, some 60 years after World War I, there still remain almost one million Canadian veterans who served their country with honour and distinction, whether on the battlefield of foreign countries or here at home, always ready to defend our proud nation.
Many of these veterans still need our help, because they returned maimed and incapacitated. Unfortunately, as the years go by, the recognition of the sacrifices of veterans diminishes; but it is all-important that we should recognize that as our veteran population grows older and passes on we must renew our efforts for increasing the needed care and attention we give to the old veteran who is left alone and to the widows who cared for their loved ones while they suffered because of war.
Finally, it is timely that this House should re-affirm Canada's commitment to its veterans. May I repeat the words of a former Prime Minister who said at Vimy Ridge in 1917:
The government and the country will consider it their first duty to see that a proper appreciation of your effort and of your courage is brought to the notice of the people at home-and it will always be our endeavour to so guide the attitude of public opinion that the country will support the government to prove to the returned men its just and due appreciation of the inestimable value of the services rendered to the country and empire and that no man will have just cause to reproach the government for having broken faith with the men who won and the men who died.

I would like to ask whether any member in this House can justify the Minister of Transport on any other minister going by Jetstar from here to Montreal and return. Here is this guy who talks about restraint and who says to my farmers that the Crowsnest rates will probably have to go, and who tells them that the user should pay the total cost of transportation, setting the most extravagant example of any minister. I say to hon. members that Jimmy Carter, the president-elect of the U.S., had the chance to take a government aircraft to his vacation spot a few weeks ago, but he said that was not proper and he was going to pay his own way when on vacation because he was not going on official government business. If that is the practice in the United States, why cannot the ministers in this government set that type of example to our people? It is beyond me why they cannot.
Perhaps I could make one more point on that subject. Some of the trips that the Minister of Transport has made are not, in my humble opinion, on government business. Last weekend he addressed a meeting of young Liberals in Saskatchewan. I understand that that type of thing has happened in the past. When he addresses a partisan political meeting of either young or old Liberals, that proportion of the flight should be paid by the minister or by the Liberal Party of Canada. If he has four meetings and one is with Liberals, the party should pay for one quarter of the cost. That would be fair.
The other point I wanted to make is that under this bill there will be a repeal of "at and east" rates. This is the rate that deals with shipment by rail of grain and flour from the Georgian Bay elevators and other elevators in Ontario to the city of Halifax and the city of Saint John in New Brunswick. The movement involves about 30 million bushels of western grain per year at a cost, in the form of a subsidy, of about $11 million to the federal government. This works out to a subsidy of about 33 cents per bushel of wheat.

There are many effects this may have on both the prairie economy and the economy in the Atlantic provinces. First of all, the Canadian Wheat Board, because of the lack of a subsidy, may halt all rail shipments from inland ports to Atlantic ports during the winter months, and they will do it because of the straight economics of moving that grain.
Second, a loss of business and employment in the elevators in Halifax and Saint John will result. We all know that the Atlantic provinces have a high rate of unemployment. The Halifax elevator is owned by the government, but CPR which owns the Saint John elevator is expected to close it down.
Finally, elevators at Georgian Bay will be put out of business since the storage and forwarding of western grain is their major source of income. It will also create additional difficulties for the Canadian Wheat Board in meeting export targets.
While the federal government people say that the Canadian Wheat Board will off-set the discontinuation of shipments in the winter months through Atlantic ports by increased shipments through Vancouver, it is obvious that in years of high volume exports the west coast ports area is already strained to capacity. Second, it does not seem reasonable to ship western grains destined for Europe through Vancouver. It would seem therefore that from now on shipments of grain to Europe will be interrupted for three months or more each year.
For reasons such as these, reasons which I think will cause difficulties to the prairie farmers and the prairie economy, and which will cause unemployment in areas where these elevators are located, particularly in Halifax and Saint John, I hope the government will reconsider the provision in the bill which deals with "at and east" rates.
In conclusion I want to say that a number of other members in my caucus have talked about other aspects of the bill before me, or will be doing so in the days to come. But I want to say that if the government seriously expects the Canadian people to support the anti-inflation program, it must start showing leadership in the House. The Minister of Transport himself must start acting like an adult, not like a little child with a toy. He has to show some leadership in the House. If that is done, then perhaps more Canadians will have confidence in the government and will not be as cynical about the political system that we have in our country. It is the type of example set by the Minister of Transport that makes people really cynical about the federal government and federal institutions. This country is too important to me and to all of us in the House for us to allow it to fall apart for reasons such as I have stated today, for lack of leadership and lack of a good example.
There are many other things that could be referred to and about which other hon. members in my party will be talking. One of them is the unemployment rate which is very high. This means that there should be more stimulation in the economy and that the government should show leadership in that direction, which it is not doing.
My time is running out, Mr. Speaker, so I will take my seat and listen to the speeches of other hon. members in the hope
November 10, 1976

that the Minister of Transport will perhaps rise and apologize to the House for his conduct, and perhaps one of the members opposite will take up my challenge and speak up on whether or not he thinks the minister should be using a private government jet to fly from here to Montreal and back.

In fact, it was because that happened to certain persons whom I knew that I went into politics and am here today.
The next thing I want to say about this statement is that when it comes to the dilemma the minister referred to near the end of his remarks about the hard choice that might have to be made between further reductions in cost and the provision of service, I hope the government will not make the kind of mistake that could result in false economy, that is, by simply trying to save more money because efficiency experts or operational performance managers decide that a number of people should be fired, with the result that poorer service is given to the people of Canada. That, in the end, will not save

money, let alone give a good name to the public service of this country.
It is important to have efficiency and to have things done according to the rule and the book, but I should like to suggest that there are times in dealing with people-and most of what the public service does is in relation to people-when sensitivity, understanding and compassion are more important than competence. So let us go for this approach and measure efficiency of our public servants, but let us not forget the fact that what we are dealing with is a human operation. The main purpose of everything done by the government and by the public service of Canada is to make life better for the persons who make up the population of this country. Let us keep the operation on that basis.
In that connection there is something else I would like to say. I hope the minister will not mind my saying it. I know, from personal conversations with the President of the Treasury Board, that he agrees with me on this. I think the time has come when the government and we in parliament should do a little more defending of the public servants of this country. I am annoyed with the one and two-page advertisements which have appeared in some of our newspapers denigrating public servants and making out that they are a pampered lot who get benefits and privileges not available to other persons. When I think of the money it costs to run those kinds of advertisements, I wonder where that money comes from. I think there are times when we ought to take a moment-and I am doing it right now-to say that those who are in the public service of this country are workers just like the workers back home in our constituencies, and we should not treat them as whipping-boys and blame them because things do not go as they ought to.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I want to thank my colleagues in the House for the opportunity to carry on. I will try to be brief.
The success of any program can only be measured by the end result, and the government's program has been a complete and absolute failure. As I indicated earlier, the bureaucratic machinery was effectively used to defuse the program. It was obvious from the outset that the complexity of the government's rural native housing program would mitigate against its success. I doubt if the government is prepared to discuss the actual implementation of the program and the numerous committees and interdepartmental committees. However, a brief glimpse at some of the components will reveal the absurdity of the structure which inevitably had to lead to its failure.
A national monitoring committee was established which ostensibly permitted native associations to watch carefully the implementation process as it progressed. The native housing group at CMHC was to establish interdepartmental and intergovernmental committees at the federal and provincial levels. On the government side, the committee structure recommended the establishment of an interdepartmental committee at the federal level to co-ordinate the activities of federal government departments such as the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, the Department of Manpower and Immigration, the Department of National Health and Welfare, the Department of the Secretary of State, and to round out the game plan
80005-S

November 18, 1976
Housing
there was the establishment of intergovernmental and interdepartmental committees to ensure that federal and provincial governments were directly involved so that they could be assured the rural and native housing groups attained their goals.
I doubt if there has ever been greater expenditure of energy, time and money for the reallocation of personnel for a specific project that has been a total failure. Is it any wonder provinces were less than enthusiastic about the program and that many delayed signing the necessary agreements? What have been some of the anticipated failures? The most obvious and inhumane is the small number of new homes built, purchased or repaired. The central concept of client involvement resulting in community development and rehabilitation was not implemented. The development of local housing societies or co-ops did not materialize to the degree anticipated. Disunity developed between provincial housing officials and native housing organizations as well as with local housing societies where they were formed. CMHC regional branch offices gave little or no encouragement to the program. I ask what the government is doing to assess the needs in respect of native housing in urban areas. Mr. Speaker, I stated in the House on November 5,
1976,	that I would be reporting on my recent talks in Paris regarding Canada-France fisheries questions. I propose to do that today, but first I think it would be useful to review in a more general way developments relating to the implementation of our 200-mile fisheries zone.
The decision to extend our fisheries zones on the Atlantic and Pacific coasts was taken in light of the urgent need to halt the rapid depletion of our fish stocks and arrest the decline of our inshore fisheries industry, a situation which had reached crisis proportions. The urgent nature of this problem required us to take action before conclusion of the Law of the Sea Conference where fisheries questions are among the many matters being discussed. Nevertheless, the new, extended jurisdiction is in conformity with the consensus emerging at the Law of the Sea Conference. The principle is now firmly embodied in the Revised Single Negotiating Text that a coastal state has the sovereign right to manage the living resources of the sea in a 200-mile zone adjacent to its shoreline. The main features of the new Canadian regime are based on the relevant provisions of the Revised Single Negotiating Text.
A number of countries have enacted, or are soon to enact, 200-mile zones, including Mexico, Norway, Denmark, France, the U.K. and the U.S.A. Most recently, the foreign ministers of the Nine agreed that a European Economic Community 200-mile fisheries zone should be in place as of January 1,
1977.	Altogether, there are now some 50 states which have
Fisheries Zones
already, or will soon establish extended Fisheries zones beyond 12 miles, and in many cases as far as 200 miles. Thus, from the standpoint of both emerging treaty law and cumulative state practices there is a sound basis in international law for the action Canada has taken to protect the living resources in waters contiguous to its shoreline.
Canada has not only acted in accordance with emerging international law but has also made every effort to take into account the interests of those states directly affected by our extended jurisdiction. We have been conscious of the need to avoid disputes with other countries stemming from our new fisheries management regime. For this reason, Canada has taken a number of steps, internationally, aimed at achieving a smooth transition to our new 200-mile jurisdiction regime.
Our first priority was to obtain agreement within ICNAF on fishing quotas for the calendar year 1977 which would correspond to Canadian requirements within the 200-mile zone. At Canada's insistence, total allowable catches of stock have been set at levels low enough to ensure rebuilding of threatened species over a period of time. There will be a further meeting of ICNAF in December, in Spain, to deal with the quotas on a few remaining stocks. I should point out for those members who perhaps are not familiar with the shorthand title of ICNAF that it is the International Commission for North Atlantic Fisheries.
The commission, at our urging, is in the process of examining the role it might play in future. We have given formal notice of Canada's intention to withdraw from the convention, as has the U.S.A. I am hopeful, however, that ICNAF can make the necessary adjustment to Canada's exclusive jurisdiction, management and enforcement in the 200-mile zone, and that the new arrangements will preserve the long tradition of international co-operation, particularly in the field of scientific research, which has grown up within the commission. On this basis Canada could continue to play a full and active part in the work of the commission. After the December meeting we will be in a better position to assess what our attitude toward ICNAF should be for the coming year.

The combined effect of proposed tariff and taxation legislation as indicated by the minister in his budget speech is a net reduction in budgetary revenues of $75 million during our current fiscal year. Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege which, as I indicated yesterday, concerns the role of parliamentary secretaries answering, at will, questions directed to ministers or acting ministers. Yesterday, questions I asked of the acting minister of finance, in the absence of the Minister of Finance, and of the Prime Minister, were answered by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance, despite the fact that repeated efforts were made to direct those questions to the acting minister of finance. These questions, in general, dealt with the intentions of the minister of bringing down a new budget, and specifically with his assessment of the economy in light of an unfavourable forecast by the OECD of the economic future of this country.
As such, these were questions of policy which in tradition, precedent and practice have been reserved for ministers and acting ministers, not parliamentary secretaries who are not privy to cabinet decisions and who do not share in the collective ministerial responsibility of government for its policies and programs.
I know that there have been exchanges on topics related to the one I am dealing with today, and I do not propose to cite examples of precedents which have already been put before Your Honour, including the precedent-as will be seen in Hansard-of October 29. I do feel, however, that budget considerations are among the clearest examples of government policy:making, and no parliamentary secretary, no matter how competent-and I stress that-can attempt to answer questions of this kind when he has no access to or responsibility for the decisions of the cabinet. If a question regarding the development of policy is asked, then the answer of a parliamentary secretary, who constitutionally has no role in discussions of policy, must of necessity be irrelevant to the question. The answer can be no more than a bland reassurance based on blissful ignorance rather than informed concern.
1370

November 25, 1976
Oral Questions
I noted with interest the exchange last month on this very point when the Chair indicated that in addition to the well-recognized right of hon. members of the House to ask questions, there is also no obligation to answer those questions. The Chair also stated, as reported at page 590 of Hansard:
-it is difficult to say that a mere attempt to answer on the part of the parliamentary secretary, acting minister or another acting in his stead is not an adequate response when no response is required by the rules.
Mr. Speaker, I believe you put your finger on a very important distinction which I would like to reiterate today. For example, this distinction was brought out in the book "Procedures in the Canadian House of Commons", written by Mr. Dawson. At page 158 of this book, Mr. Dawson discusses the whole question of the impact of the question period. He points out that the rules certainly contemplate that information is solicited and, hopefully, gained. But in reference to Your Honour's comment of October 29, I think Mr. Dawson's opinion is very relevant, and that opinion is expressed at page 158. Referring to the detail we solicit as far as questions are concerned, Mr. Dawson states:
This is, however, the most limited and least valuable use of the parliamentary question. There is little doubt that a letter or telephone call to a minister would produce factual information more quickly than would a question in the House. The rules, of course, ignore the real purpose of most questions. Over the years they have become the principal weapon in the hands of the opposition parties. There is little hope in their minds that they will get a major amendment accepted in the House or otherwise alter government policy significantly. They may, however, harass the government and demonstrate its deficiencies to the electorate. For this the oral parliamentary question is unequalled. The question itself must be short but each answer as it comes from the minister can be... followed to a conclusion whether that conclusion be a revelation by the government of all the significant facts, or perhaps, even more revealing, a refusal to disclose them.
I suggest that that is a fundamental reason why it has become customary that the rules provide that oral questions be put only to ministers and, as is accepted, to acting ministers. They, and they alone, should be tested in this House. I suggest that the demonstration we had in the oral question period today is a vivid demonstration. The President of the Treasury Board and the Prime Minister were under an oral question barrage which, I suggest, had a totally different effect in its outcome on this House than if that exchange had been directed to parliamentary secretaries on behalf of those two gentlemen.

I withdraw. If the hon. member for Crowfoot says that he did not take a side either way, this is the first time in his life he has done so. He is an outspoken person who does not hesitate to take a stand on any issue. However, I take him at his word and I have no quarrel with that. If it was just a question he was asking, that is fine.
The interest we are expressing in this matter has to go beyond 12,000 shareholders. It has to ask the question of how it affects Canadians generally. It raises some very important issues above the question of the shareholders. It is easy to understand why the shareholders want to convert themselves into a bank. As one of the officers of the bank replied in the finance committee a few weeks ago, "We want to play in the major leagues". I do not hold it against anyone playing in the major leagues, if that is what they want to do. There is no doubt that moving into the major leagues would be immensely profitable for IAC and its shareholders. That is enough reason for them to approve the bid to convert into a bank. But shareholders' profit is not a reason that should be so compelling to parliament. In order for parliament to pass this bill, it should satisfy itself that the bill is in the public interest. Up until this point that has not been demonstrated to me or to my colleagues.
I admire the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River. I have known him for a long time. I appreciate his sincerity in putting forward his arguments. However, I wish he would have a somewhat better cause than the one he is advocating today.
Let me quote from the Financial Post of April 3, 1976, to reinforce the argument I am trying to make, that the issue of the national interest is not at all clear. If it is not clear to the Financial Post, how can it be clear to anyone? While someone might want to quarrel with my perspective, vision or idea of clarity, surely the vision of clarity of the Financial Post is of a somewhat different order. I quote:
Clearly, the IAC-Continental stall-
That refers to the national interest debate which the NDP is carrying on.
-raises some serious questions for the financial system as a whole-questions that will certainly get important billing during the forthcoming Bank Act debate.
At issue: is it in the public interest for a large, efficient financial organization to convert to a chartered bank? If so, what special arrangements should be permitted to allow for an orderly transition, and what time limit should be set?
If our arguments for waiting until the Bank Act was concluded were valid before, they are even more valid at this point. I imagine within weeks the government will be referring the Bank Act or, more likely, the white paper on banking to the finance committee for examination. If the IAC conversion bill is passed, what is the point of having a debate on the Bank Act? All that IAC is asking for to convert itself into a bank is all contained in the stuff and substance of the debate on the Bank Act. If we pass this bill, we may as well forget about passing the Bank Act.
It is arrogant for a corporation like IAC to come before parliament to ask for special privileges in advance of legislation. The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River argued that they are very much in line with the white paper and very much in line with what the government will probably do with amendments to the Bank Act. Therefore, he said, why not let them have it now, rather than wait until the Bank Act is concluded? There are a number of things to be said about that.
What would the hon. member say if in the process of debating a bill to increase the old age pension or amend the Canada Pension Plan a pensioner petitioned this House saying that he had a terrible need and could not wait for the debate to be concluded in parliament as that might take a whole year? He may point out that he has to pay his rent for this month, and as members know, if the bill is passed he would like his cheque right now. I would be far more sympathetic in that case than in this case. This is true of every piece of legislation.
Suppose we were in the process of debating an amendment to the Criminal Code. During the course of that debate, would we instruct the judges, saying that that portion of the Criminal Code is being amended and, therefore, "Do not register any convictions under that section"? That would be an affront to parliament. We would call it arrogant. That is particularly true in this case as it was made quite clear the last time that as far as we were concerned the bill was not going to pass, and we gave our reasons for it.
It bothers me to some extent. I am not the type of person who normally likes to dig in or embarrass anyone or even to say, "Look, I am doing it to inconvenience business." If business comes to me or to other people in my party, we are quite willing to listen and be accommodating to the extent it is possible. If the interests of business and the interests of the country can be demonstrated, we are not going to put up a great fuss. The point is that such a relationship is not clear in this case. There is something about this whole thing that puts me on edge.
What bothers me is that the people in IAC, highly intelligent people, obviously able to run a very large corporation and make a success of it, simply do not understand a darned thing about parliament. They think that if they want something, they can come here and get it without any great debate

The Prime Minister says that is clear. It certainly was not clear in his opening statement in which he said he had to go to another meeting.
Mr. Speaker, there are a number of points which have to be cleared up, and I hope they can be cleared up later. The first is whether the letter to which the Prime Minister referred is the same letter to which the former auditor general was referring. He makes the very serious statement that he wrote privately to the Prime Minister suggesting that he had information indicating that Canadian Crown corporations were paying bribes to foreign buyers to sell certain products. That is a serious charge.
If there is another letter, I think Mr. Henderson ought to have the opportunity to appear before the public accounts committee, if he is willing to appear, to produce such a letter. Certainly, the Prime Minister has the obligation to have his staff search further to see whether such letter exists. The second thing we ought to know is whether the invoices are being tabled and whether they deal with any company or Crown corporation other than the CDC, which is apparently the only company regarding which Mr. Drury, who was then president of the treasury board, made any inquiries. That matter should be cleared up.
I support the suggestion made, that the terms of reference of the public accounts committee should be widened. That committee has not yet sat. The terms of reference will be, as I understand them, the public accounts and the Auditor General's report. But the matters to which Mr. Maxwell Henderson refers, of course, have much wider scope and cover a different period of time. Therefore, I think the public accounts committee, on the government's initiative-and there will have to be a motion in the House-should be given the widest possible latitude in order to allow Mr. Henderson to appear, to allow the Prime Minister to appear, to ascertain whether there is a letter other than that which the Prime Minister tabled this morning, and to find out whether Mr. Henderson has any substantial evidence to corroborate the statements he makes when he claims that he wrote to the Prime Minister saying that he had information which led him to believe that certain Canadian Crown corporations were using bribes.
Oral Questions
I think this matter cannot be settled simply by a statement by the Prime Minister. We are prepared to accept the statement that this is the only correspondence he can find, but it seems to me, in view of the seriousness of the charge and in view of the person from whom it comes, that this matter ought to have very thorough investigation by the public accounts committee, on the basis of widened terms of reference, so that there will not be any nit-picking as to whether that committee has full authority to go back to some period in time in order to look into this matter and related matters regarding agents who have been used by Crown corporations and have submitted accounts which have been called in question, not just by Mr. Maxwell Henderson but by the present Auditor General.

Mr. Speaker, at five o'clock I was talking about the voluntary restraints that were implemented by the Post Office Department and what I thought was the unreasonable position in which that placed many people in this country. I was talking about developments in the cities and what happens when there is a restraint program arbitrarily agreed to within a department which affects areas where development takes place after the imposition of the controls.
The point I was trying to make was that the injury resulted when one project or one district had been completed and mail delivery service had been instituted in that area, but because of the imposition of a restraint program a few months or a few weeks later, an adjacent area which had taken longer to develop and become a fully residential area was denied the same service simply because it was caught in the middle of the program. This kind of program is unfair and unwarranted. A cut-back in any department should be of such a nature that it does not discriminate, and it must have the same impact on all.
In the last decade even though the Post Office Department has experienced a 50 per cent increase in staff and a 50 per cent increase in the cost of operation, together with a recent increase in the price of postage, it is strange that the service has deteriorated to an intolerable level. There is no question in my mind that some form of action on the part of the government is long overdue.

Bill C-19 is an attempt to plug a leak in the dike. I want to talk for a few minutes about the Company of Young Canadians that was brought into being by the late Lester B. Pearson. The tale is told in a book entitled "The Big Rip-off," written by a lady by the name of Erna Koffman. It clearly illustrates the fumbling, bumbling, mismanagement, deceit, and distortion which took place not only within the confines of the political offices responsible for the program but also within the sanctions of the public servants responsible for its administration. In retrospect one would think that the players in this CYC game outside the realm of politics were selected on the basis of their incompetence to perform within the intent of the legislation, with unexcelled competence to milk the system.
No one was more pleased than I to see the Company of Young Canadians go down the pipe, regrettably too late, after the program had cost the people of Canada millions of dollars. What did Erna Koffman say about the program and some of its activities? How did the program work? For the record I should like to read one paragraph from the book "The Big Rip-off' which I think deals very clearly with how responsible were the administrators of that program. Theoretically, any community in Canada that wanted to embark on a self-help programme could request the services of a 'volunteer' of the CYC. However, since shortly after its inception, the CYC has run into flak, and criticism has poured into Ottawa from many parts of the country where the CYC has been operating, accusing the Company of stirring up trouble or encouraging troublesome elements in Communities. The Premier of one Western Province ordered the Company out of his province. It seems that wherever there are civic disturbances, CYC workers seem to be around.
We talk about restraint, yet this government put millions of dollars into a program which was responsible for this kind of activity.
I wonder if the government still thinks that a comptroller general, a chief financial officer, could not have prevented this kind of waste of public funds relative to this program. We do not need a royal commission to tell us that a program is wrong in principle, that it is mismanaged and far too expensive. Mr. Speaker, on this point I think you find yourself and the House finds itself in a somewhat narrow dilemma. I have had to deal with this problem in the past, and in view of the fact that the working copies, or what we call the "blues", go to the press gallery and are used as the basis for press stories, I suggest it is not the right argument to say that those copies are irrelevant.

There were times when people were being very improper when making catcalls, but they were sitting in, shall we say, the privileged circle, within the hearing of the reporters who develop an ear for a particular voice and are able to take down remarks which may not be heard in the far reaches of the chamber; so these remarks appear in Hansard. They are not known to the speaker, nor has the Chair had a chance to hear them.
While we can say that the blues are not the final proof, I can say that Hansard tomorrow will not necessarily reflect what was actually said. I have seen amended "blues" where whole phrases and paragraphs have been blue-pencilled. They have been blue-pencilled either by the individual who made the remarks or by someone on his staff. There have been many instances of that.
In addition, if it is valid for this House to consider that one of the working copies, a green copy, shall be forwarded to the press as its working document-and no one objects to that- how can we in our, shall we say, sanctity ignore those copies when it might happen that tomorrow the official record of what was said will not disclose that the phrase was used at all, notwithstanding the fact that the government House leader says he heard it? The opposition House leader says he heard it, and the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants (Mr. McCleave), who raised the question of privilege, says he heard it; yet it is conceivable that it will not appear in the official record. The hon. member for Scarborough East (Mr. O'Connell) may shake his head, but it is a fact. Therefore, I suggest that the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants was correct in saying that reference would have to be made to the working copies and not just to Hansard.

Mr. Speaker, as Dr. Ollivier, former joint law clerk of the House of Commons, said at page 85 of the report on the British North America Act in 1935:
Confederation is a union of independent and sovereign states bound together by a pact or a treaty for the observance of certain conditions dependent upon the unanimous consent of the contracting parties who are free to withdraw from the union.
This definition indicates that the status of sovereignty must precede confederation and that a federal union can be consummated only by the mutual consent of contracting states adopting a constitution.
Mr. Speaker, from the evidence which I have thus far submitted, I draw the following conclusions: first, the provinces of Canada desired a federal union; second, the Quebec resolutions provided for a federal union; third, the bill drafted by the Canadian delegates at the London conference also provided for a federal union; fourth, the Colonial Office was not disposed to grant the provinces of Canada their request for a federal union; fifth, the British North America Act, enacted by the imperial parliament, carried out neither the spirit nor the terms of the Quebec resolutions; sixth, Canada did not become a federal union under the British North America Act but, rather, a united colony. The privilege of federating, therefore, was still a future privilege.
Seventh, the parliament of Canada did not become the government of Canada, much less a federal government. It became merely the central legislature of a united colony, a legislative body whose only power was that of aiding and advising the governor general as agent of the imperial parliament. Eight, the British North America Act, as enacted by the imperial parliament, was not a constitution but merely an act of the imperial parliament which united four colonies in Canada into one colony with the supreme authority still remaining in the hands of the British government.

December 3, 1976
The Constitution

Mr. Speaker, of all the debates held on the history of Canada, the constitutional debate seems to be recurring most often. Although the opinions which were voiced here are most shocking, they nevertheless reflect what I consider as the only truth. However, we should not believe they are unfounded revelations since they are shared and have been made public by people whose competence is well known such as Dr. Ollivi-er, Doctor of Laws and former law expert in the House of Commons, Dr. Scantland, former Secretary of State for External Affairs and Mr. Beauchesne, former clerk of the House of Commons, who appeared as witnesses before the Special Committee on the British North America Act of 1935. Further, the opinions voiced are similar to those expressed by Professor Roger Smith, an expert on constitutional matters and Mr. W. Kool, Member of Parliament for Jasper-Edson in the 40's.
Mr. Speaker, the remarks I am making today are the result of ten years of intensive research and are based on undeniable sources of work, research and competence. The British North America Act was nothing else than the recognition of a unified North American colony under the authority of the Imperial government in London. Moreover, this Act did not allow the formation of a government as such, but rather that of a Central Parliament and Provincial Legislatures subject to England. The statute of sovereign government would have given the provinces their sovereignty if the British Parliament had granted their request for a federal union.
But this sovereignty only remained a remote possibility because, by refusing to form a real confederation, the English Parliament denied the provinces the right to create:
A Union of Confederation of sovereign states created by treaty or by mutual adoption of a federal Constitution . ..
-according to the definition found in Mr. Bouvier's law dictionary.
It is therefore obvious that following the English refusal, Canada was not in 1867 a Confederation as requested in the Quebec resolutions, because the British North America Act should have been based on the Quebec and not the London conference. Indeed, while the Quebec resolutions contained 72 paragraphs, the British North America Act contains 147 paragraphs, that is more than twice as much.
Secondly, the so-called constitution of the British North America Act is not a contract between the provinces, since in 1867 no agreement had been reached among them. The most obvious evidence of that lies in the BNA Act having been amended six times between 1871 and 1918, namely in 1871, 1875, 1886, 1907, 1915 and 1918, five of which without the consent of or even consultation with the provinces.
This is indeed contrary to the concept of a contract or a confederative pact, as mentioned on page 59 of the Special Committee report on the British North America Act.

Clearly, what we need to do is not to pass the buck on to the provinces but, instead, exercise national leadership to try to bring together the efforts at restraint to all levels of government.

December 9, 1976
Economic Policy

There is another major difference between our approach and theirs, that is, the relation between the federal spending policy and that of the other levels of government. One of the favorite tackles of this government in limiting its expenditures is quite senselessly to shift its commitments on the provinces, and to hell with the taxpayers: they have no choice but to support all governments.
In our approach, we endeavour to generate a coordinated and joint effort on the part of all levels of government with a view to moderating the overall demand on the economy. I underestimate neither the difficulty nor the complexity of that endeavour, but it is necessary: otherwise, we will witness no less than the abdication of the leadership.
This brings me to the second point I want to stress in this context. It is obvious for everybody, except the government, that we cannot continue making decisions which affect more than two fifths of our national economy on the basis of the arbitrary and unilateral action of eleven different governments. And yet that is what we do in Canada. The federal and provincial governments make their budgetary decisions separately, without real co-ordination, which often puts them in competition, if not in opposition.

Of course, the ministers of finance meet, as they did earlier this week. But I do not think any of us would pretend, in the present atmosphere, that they even seek to achieve any meaningful co-ordination of the economic direction of what amounts to two fifths of our national output. This, clearly, is not a one-sided affair. The fault-if that is the term I should use-does not rest solely with the federal government. The government has contributed-significantly to the whole problem of governments acting unilaterally in a country requiring co-operation, but it is not the exclusive agent of that kind of action.
It is fair to assert, however, that only the federal government can show the kind of national leadership we need if we are to achieve worth-while economic co-ordination within the public sector. Along with maintaining security, the management of the national economy is probably the most fundamental responsibility of the federal government. It controls the monetary system, and while it does not by any means exercise all the fiscal power, it controls the national fiscal lever and thus, in a very real way, sets the framework for everyone else. Only the national government can exercise the primary responsibility for economic management in Canada.
In the name of that responsibility there must be a much greater effort, a much more concerted active national leadership in seeking to co-ordinate, through consensus and through compromise, the impact of public sector policies and demands upon our economy as a whole. That will mean, not a giving up of ultimate responsibility by the government of Canada but a greater willingness on the part of all governments to act as partners and to share information and planning before each exercises the responsibility which ultimately rests with each.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to speak briefly on Bill C-209. I want to commend the hon. member for Toronto-Lakeshore (Mr. Robinson) for proposing this legislation. I must confess to him that when I first saw that there was a bill dealing with noise pollution, I thought it was to reform the rules of the House. I was pleasantly surprised to learn that the bill deals with the problem of noise pollution in factories.
The hon. member deserves a great deal of credit for the comments in his speech on second reading of the bill. 1 think he explained the bill extremely well. As the hon. member explained, the purpose of the bill is to deal with the problem of noise pollution in industrial plants. He explained the bill quite fully, and I do not propose to take a great deal of time. I certainly do not want to be responsible for preventing the bill from coming to a vote this afternoon.
There is a growing recognition on the part of Canadians throughout this country that there are tremendous problems caused by noise pollution in factories and by noise pollution generally. In recent years there has been an awareness of the problems of environmental health hazards and of the effects that noise pollution can have on one's hearing, on one's general health and also upon one's ability to work. The fact is that studies have shown that where workers are asked to work under conditions which are unfavourable and which are very unpleasant for them, the quality of their work deteriorates. Anything we as a parliament can do to improve employment standards for people in Canada and to improve their productivity and health should be done.
I think there is also a general recognition on the part of business that anything that can be done by businesses to improve the working conditions of their employees should be done, and I think there is a willingness to comply wherever possible with what is being suggested in this bill. 1 think the hon. member recognized in the comments he made that there would be instances in which there would be difficulties for industries in complying with the provisions of the bill. Obviously, there are some industries in which it is simply impossible-for example, in heavy industries dealing with metal or in industries where people work around aircraft-to lower the noise level to below 85 decibels. However, the hon. member
Social Health
quite properly suggested that in those instances the employees involved should be provided with protective devices which would give some protection to their eardrums and which would prevent them from being damaged. If the provisions of the bill were applied flexibly, no undue burden need be put upon employers. The bill could also do a great deal to encourage employers who really are not concerned about the well-being of their employees to take some action.
The hon. member noted that under the terms of the British North America Act it is likely that the responsibility for legislation with regard to noise levels in industry falls under provincial jurisdiction. Obviously, the parliament of Canada cannot legislate a national standard for noise pollution in factories and force it upon the provinces. To do so would be improper and an intrusion on provincial jurisdiction. It would obviously be illegal, as well. However, what the hon. member tries to do in his bill is come in, perhaps through the back door, and set standards of behaviour for factories which are doing work on behalf of the federal government. That might encourage the provinces to take some action as well. I think that is a sensible way of dealing with this problem.
This bill would only take effect in cases where there are federal contracts involved with industries, and this could be a condition of the contracts. I do not think, in my reading of the bill, that this maximum noise level is compulsory in all contracts, but it could be a condition of a contract between the federal government and a private employer that the noise level in the factory to which employees would be subjected would have to be 85 decibels or lower. Let us suppose that at age 65 he finds that he must withdraw some money from his RRSP savings. Is he permitted to make piecemeal withdrawals when he reaches 65 or over and pay tax only on that portion that he withdraws?
December 15, 1976

After all, if the RRSP has a purpose, it is the accumulation of funds which would be spread over his retirement years. If at age 65 he cannot withdraw some portion for that year's use without paying tax on the total in the RRSP, it is really defeating the purpose of the initial savings that he made. It seems to me that he should only pay tax on that portion that he must withdraw in any given year after reaching 65. This would then put it in a position comparable to a pension. As the hon. member for Ottawa said, and also the minister, in many instances these plans are in lieu of a pension. If a man is to be penalized for withdrawing any portion on an annual basis, then it does not conform with the concept of a pension.

Mr. Chairman, I welcome the opportunity to make a few comments on Bill C-22, to amend the Income Tax Act. There are a number of provisions in this bill about which 1 have a great deal of concern and to which I take some objection because in my opinion some of the amendments proposed only perpetuate some of the inequities in our personal income tax system which discriminate against low and middle income Canadians, to the advantage of upper income Canadians. For this reason I would like to outline, first of all in a general way, my philosophical reasons for objecting to some of these clauses, and then to get into some specifics and deal with some of the amendments before us.
In any income tax system that any government imposes, there seems to be an obligation on the part of the government to have some kind of fairness and equity in the system so that groups and different sectors will bear the burden of taxes in proportion to their ability to pay. We have in this country the personal income tax system and the corporate income tax system. What has been happening to various tax policies of the government-and the bill before us today is only the latest example-is a change in the tax burden, in who is shouldering this burden.
What has happened, for example, is that over the past couple of decades we have seen a change in the way that the corporate sector bears the tax burden and the way in which the person or individual citizen in Canada has to pay taxes. For example, in the 1951-1952 fiscal year we find that about 54 per cent of the income tax collected by the federal government came from the corporate sector, and about 46 per cent of taxes came from personal income taxes. But a couple of decades later, by 1973-74, this proportion had changed dramatically, for in that year, the latest for which statistics are available, we find that about 30 per cent of income taxes came from the corporations and about 70 per cent came from individuals.
So a great shift has taken place in the income tax system. The burden has been shifted to individuals, to the personal income tax system and away from the corporate income tax system. The point is that this shift has come away from the corporate sector to the personal income sector at the same time that corporate profitability has been increasing, and hence their ability to share the burden has been enhanced. We find, for example, in the last five-year period from 1970 to 1975 that corporations' profits have increased from $7.7 billion to $17.8 billion, or an increase of 131 per cent. But during the same period of increased corporate profitability the corporate tax rate declined from the effective rate of 29.6 per cent to 26.6 per cent.
Estimates show that because of the tax concessions, the write-offs and the loopholes, the federal treasury has been losing some $2 billion to $3 billion a year in terms of the corporate tax revenue that it could be collecting. On top of this kind of inequity there has also been another provision which has allowed corporations to postpone or defer paying income taxes, a provision which is not available to individual Canadi-
Income Tax
ans. To date we have the astounding figure-they are estimates, but based on the rate of deferral-that corporations have been able to defer or avoid paying the federal treasury some $10 billion in corporate income tax. That is a very significant sum. We do not even charge interest at the going rate on this deferral of some $10 billion. It is, in effect, a free loan; but you know very well that if I were to be late in paying my personal income tax, I would be charged interest on it.
The argument for this reduction in the corporate tax rate as well as the shift of the tax burden away from corporations to personal income taxes has always been that this will stimulate the economy and create more jobs. What a hollow and false argument that has proved to be. We find that some 700,000 Canadians are unemployed today. Obviously, the tax concession method is not working to promote a healthy economy for Canadians. The point is that we have a system of taxation which has built-in inequities with regard to the corporate and personal income tax systems which are further compounded when we analyse the trends which have been taking place within the personal income tax system itself. What I am trying to show is that the burden has been shifted away from corporation taxes to personal income taxes, and within the personal income tax system the burden is being shifted away from those in upper income brackets to those in lower and middle income brackets. RRSPs are only one example of the inequities that are taking place in our income tax system.

Mr. Speaker, it is a great and exhilarating experience to speak in the House of Commons on a Tuesday night just before the Christmas recess.
I will not be too long in my remarks. There are several others who wish to speak and I think they will all be reasonably short because I believe there is a disposition to move with some haste on this piece of legislation.

His predecessor did not appear to have the same recognition of the suggestion that this matter be aired here in this House rather than proceeded with by way of order in Council.

I have not been at all impressed by some of the information that has come out of the Metric Commission, and all of us continue to get mail criticizing the fact that we are proceeding with this conversation. Generally speaking I think everyone supports the idea or concept of metric conversion, yet we find in talking to various ministers that they still want to proceed in this rather cavalier and high-handed way. The point I have tried to make in the past is that the best way to get the metric conversion settled is by having a wide open debate in the House so that interested people can speak on the measure. Let us get things out in the open. This would do a great deal of good, much more than some of the promotional material from the Metric Commission.
I would caution the minister that when he introduces another bill he should not leave it until the 11th hour. We recognize that this bill must be passed. We are going to recess soon, to return in late January, and this is supposed to be in

effect on February 1. However, I think the bill could have been introduced one, two or three weeks ago. Certainly it was before us on November 22. I hope the next time around the minister will bring his bill in for debate in the proper way. I do not think that would involve too much time in the House, but there are members who have some misconceptions about metric conversion. I am sure they would like to be heard and to put forward the views of their constituents.
I think the minister and I have a slight disagreement in respect of countries, but there are only a few countries in the world not now on the metric system. I think this is a progressive step for us to take in order to complete our conversion. This bill amends several acts. I think it is pretty straightforward. It changes some of the designations in the Canadian Wheat Board Act and a few other acts dealing with grain. For example, it changes "acres" as it appears in various statutes to "hectares". The new term is a combination of the words "hecto" and "ares", "hecto" meaning "hundred" and "ares", which I think is of Greek origin, meaning a square unit and from which is derived the word "area". So the definitions are pretty straightforward. The word "bushels" is changed to "tonnes". That is an old English term. The old English is "tunne" and the middle English is "tonne".

The metric designation for pressure is "newtons per square metre" or "dynes per square centi-metre". They are used to working with one term and then, all of a sudden, another one is thrown at them and they cannot figure out what it means. I have received letters from engineers and people in the scientific field, and they have asked me what the term kilopascals means. Mr. Speaker, I wish to announce a change in Canada's nuclear export policy, a matter of central concern to the people and Government of Canada, raising as it does funda-
Nuclear Exports
mental issues affecting world economic growth and world peace.
In this Christmas season our thoughts naturally turn to peace and the brotherhood of man. It is easy to pay tribute to these fundamental goals with words. It is more important that we do so with our actions. It is a challenge to the Government of Canada to respond to the demand of Canadian public opinion that this country exercise its influence tov.ard the betterment of the global society in which we and our descendants must live. In the area of nuclear policy there is no simple answer or it would have long since been adopted. It is rather the need to balance energy requirements, the advance of technology which regardless of what we do will make nuclear capability within the reach of a wider and wider group of countries, and the need to establish a sound international framework which will curb the spread of nuclear weapons and yet take into account the legitimate economic aspirations of sovereign states. I wish to make quite clear, however, that the first priority, indeed the overriding priority, is to prevent the spread of instruments of destruction.
In this context I am pleased to announce that the Canadian government has decided upon a further strengthening of the safeguards requirements which apply to the export of Canadian reactors and uranium. Shipments to non-nuclear weapon states under future contracts will be restricted to those which ratify the Non-Proliferation Treaty or otherwise accept international safeguards on their entire nuclear program. It follows from this policy that Canada will terminate nuclear shipments to any non-nuclear weapon state which explodes a nuclear device.
This requirement is in addition to those outlined in December, 1974. The purpose of the Canadian safeguards policy is simple and straightforward. We wish to avoid contributing to the proliferation of nuclear weapons while at the same time satisfying the legitimate requirements for uranium and technology of countries which demonstrate the intention of restricting Canadian assistance only to peaceful non-explosive uses. Nuclear export policy already requires binding assurances that what Canada provides will not be used for explosive purposes. Existing policy, however, does not cover what a country receives from other suppliers or what it might do on its own. The new policy will close this gap. We will have, therefore, assurance by treaty that Canada's nuclear customers will have been selected from those countries which have made a clear and unequivocal commitment to the non-proliferation of nuclear weapons.
The development of the CANDU reactor has been one of Canada's great technological achievements. This technology is needed to reduce the world's dependence on oil. Moreover, our industrialized trading partners look to Canada as a source of uranium to fuel the nuclear reactor programs which they, like ourselves, have undertaken to meet a growing share of energy needs. In the absence of alternative technologies, developing countries will also look to nuclear power once they have exploited other conventional energy resources and have built up the national power grids necessary for large present reac-

tors. While research into conservation and renewable energy technologies should be intensified, energy planning in Canada and elsewhere must look to energy resources presently available.
While the Canadian government recognizes the legitimate energy requirements of its trading partners, it is determined to do everything within its power to avoid contributing to nuclear weapons proliferation. It is for this reason that the Government of Canada has unilaterally decided to strengthen further Canada's safeguards requirements. As in the past we are prepared to accept the commercial consequences of being clearly ahead of other suppliers. This is the price we are prepared to pay to curb the threat to mankind of nuclear proliferation.
We recognize that for this policy to be fully effective we must persuade other nuclear suppliers to adopt similar export policies. We are charting a course which we hope will serve as a compelling example for other nuclear suppliers.

Broadcasting House Proceedings

Since, after examining these difficulties, I am left with some considerable doubt, I thought it appropriate to indicate to those hon. members involved that I would invite argument on the matter at this time. I would hope to give consideration to the arguments presented and render a decision before five o'clock this afternoon.
The hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker).
