The hon. member gave the Chair notice, pursuant to Standing Order 26, of his intention to raise this matter. He has put forward a motion which relates to three questions. One has to do with a threat to Canadian confederation; second, the election of a separatist government in Quebec; and, third, the failure of the Prime Minister to inform the House-if I may quote from the motion-what steps he proposes to take to counter the threat to confederation, and so on. With regard to the first two questions, subparagraph (16) of Standing Order 26 reads as follows:
The right to move the adjournment of the House for the above purposes is subject to the following conditions:
(a) the matter proposed for discussion must relate to a genuine emergency
calling for immediate and urgent consideration-
I interpret that language as meaning that an order for debate cannot proceed if the subject suggested, however important or pressing, does not constitute an emergency but is a matter of a continuing nature. The motion expresses an opinion-and I stress that it is the hon. member's opinion- that the result of the Quebec election constitutes a threat to

confederation. But the hon. member must surely realize that if it is a threat to confederation, it is a continuing threat and not one of an emergency nature as envisaged in subsection (a) of section 16 of the Standing Order. Therefore, I would refrain from granting the special debate pursuant to Standing Order 26 on that basis. Furthermore, I am most reluctant to enter into an expression of opinion as to whether or not an election that has taken place in any province, being a duly lawful and proper election within the procedures known under our system, can, as an opinion of the Chair, constitute what is required by the Standing Order to be an emergency calling for immediate and urgent consideration.
In the final analysis, the hon. member moves from those two points to concentrate in the motion on the failure of the Prime Minister to tell this House what steps he is taking to counteract the results of this election. In that respect, while I would not say so except with the very greatest reluctance, since that is a criticism of the Prime Minister I would have to consider, under section (5) of the Standing Order, whether that is a very proper use of the allotted days that will be following.
I am very reluctant to use the escape under Standing Order 26 that so long as an opposition day remains there is a chance to discuss matters of importance, and therefore the rule ought not to be used to set up a debate. Standing Order 26 was changed in order, I think, to remove debate on whether or not the order should go, and to set up hours that could be used by the Chair which are auxiliary hours to the regular sittings. I think those changes were made in order to see that matters of national importance which ought to be debated in this chamber and which would not likely be debated in other ways could be debated under the application of the order.
I do not like to refute that by saying that since an opposition day may be coming up, that notice ought to be taken. I think that forces upon the opposition an obligation which is not natural with respect to the use of those days. However, that part of the hon. member's motion which seeks to criticize the Prime Minister for his failure to make a disclosure to this House seems to me to be a very proper use of one of the opposition days. Therefore, having regard to the two reasons that I cited previously relative to subsection (16)(a), and for the latter reason relative to section (5) of the rule, I do not see fit to set aside special hours pursuant to Standing Order 26 to debate the motion put forward by the hon. member.

Mr. Speaker, in view of alarming reports in regard to the possibility of an energy shortage which would seriously affect all Canadians, I should like to register my concern over the government's lack of a clear energy policy. The recent report of the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development has called for new government policies for conservation and energy development to head off shortages, but I wonder whether the government of Canada has taken heed. The government of Canada has a moral obligation to answer the question: how are we going to meet our energy needs, and to what extent?
For the record, Mr. Speaker, the OECD has urged its members, Canada included, to develop additional energy supplies by implementing such policies as providing incentives for improvements in oil recovery and support programs. Measures to increase production should be aimed at improving the climate for investment. That certainly is not the case at present in Canada. In many respects the government is hindering development through excessive regulations. The reaction of the government to energy problems has been to regulate. Virtually every aspect of the Canadian petroleum industry is

now tightly regulated. Canadians should really be concerned that one of our major industries is subject to regulations that are often unstable, unclear, and unco-ordinated to the point where the industry's performance is impaired.
The government must take a great deal of the blame for Canada's energy problems. Rather than assisting the oil industry by working in a spirit of co-operation on a problem that is vital to our nation, this government has put obstacles in the way of developing a positive energy policy.
The question of energy policy in the present and the future is among the most important issues facing Canada at this time. To most Canadians, energy policy is wrapped up in pricing- what we pay for home heating, electricity, of at the gasoline puihps. The government cannot hide from the fact that there is an energy shortage, and Canadians want to know what it intends to do about it. In 1974, Canada ceased being a net crude oil exporter. In 1975, Canada imported an average of 115 million barrels of crude oil per day. While Canada still exports 39 per cent of its natural gas production, this is expected to decline in the mid-1980's and create a serious balance of payments problem. Even by 1980 Canada is forecast to spend over $3 billion yearly for imported oil. Forecasts show the situation becoming progressively worse in the 1980's.
In addition to hindering the energy problem through excessive regulations, the government has also taken a large portion of revenue from the oil industry which could well be used in expanding the oil industry to meet rising energy demands. It must be pointed out that by far the greatest bulk of price increases in oil of late have resulted from increased government taxes. For instance, fully 60 per cent of the cost of a gallon of gas at the pump is federal, provincial of municipal tax. Only 38 per cent of the cost covers the oil itself, its refining, marketing, the dealer's wage, etc. Profit is approximately 2 per cent of the price. I for one reject the idea that the oil industry is enjoying excessive profits. The oil industry today is in worse position than it was prior to the fall of 1973. when the wellhead price of a barrel of crude oil was $3.
Taxes and royalties now consume, for example, about $6 of the $9.75 for a barrel of Alberta crude oil. After taxes, Mr. Speaker, the oil companies have little left for oil exploration and development. What can be said with certainty is that oil exploration costs are skyrocketing, not just because of inflation but because today drilling is at expensive sites since cheaper sites have already been explored. Returns from money invested in oil exploration are quite low compared to other investment opportunities. This too has discouraged investment in exploration. On top of all of that oil company profits are quite variable due to the uncertain nature of production.
While the energy problem continues to become serious, many Canadians are wondering what the government intends to do. Should we satisfy our energy needs from our own resources to the full extent possible at costs that offer Canada an economic advantage? I think most Canadians would answer yes, and yet the government is showing no leadership in developing such a policy. I would guarantee that our energy
Adjournment Debate
needs are met and mitigate the risks associated with massive oil imports.
As we all know, oil is a non-renewable resource. Canada's energy priorities should include an effort to minimize our use of energy. Producing our own energy resources where the costs are right may offer tremendous economic savings and benefits, but wringing out the waste in our use of energy offers even greater economic savings and benefits. Simply stated, our energy conservation objective should be the use of the minimum amount of energy required to meet our social and economic needs and aspirations. Conservation, however, cannot answer all of our energy needs.
In terms of the many challenges which today confront Canada, energy is only one challenge, but it will have inevitable effects on all the others. While there are no easy nor instant solutions to our energy challenge, that is not an excuse for the government to ignore the problem and drift along hoping the problem will solve itself.
As I stated earlier, the government has a moral obligation to answer the question of how we are going to meet our energy needs. If it does have a long range contingency plan, then it should be made public. Canadians will not tolerate secrecy on such a vital matter. I rather suspect, however, that it is not a case of secrecy but rather of no policy. I would urge the government to develop a clear policy for energy before it is too late.

Income Tax Act

I appreciate the consideration of my colleagues and I shall try not to abuse it. I was listing the revenue which would be lost to the provinces of Atlantic Canada, and Quebec, because of the changes in the unemployment insurance law as proposed by the Conservative party and accepted by the Liberal government. Nova Scotia would lose between $9 million and $11 million for the coming year, and New Brunswick between $19 million and $22 million. In the province of Quebec, about which the leader of the opposition (Mr. Clark) rightly said we should be particularly concerned at this point in our history, the loss will be between $93 million and $102 million. This money would be directly beneficial to the families suffering from unemployment. It would also have a good effect on the economy, because these people, if they got the money, would be spending it.
We have said that something has to be done about unemployment. We say it should have been done last fall, two weeks ago, last week. We shall be happy if the minister will act next week. Maybe he will be moved now that the figure of over one million Canadians unemployed has sunk into his mind with all

its human implications. We have called for direct tax cuts for people in the low and medium income brackets who will spend the money and stimulate the economy which at the present time is only operating at 85 per cent of capacity in the manufacturing centre.
We have called for the reactivation of government work programs which were put aside during the period of restraint, programs which would stimulate expansion at the municipal level across Canada. Third, we have called for a significant increase in home construction, low income housing, to meet both the need of job creation and the human need for decent accommodation. Finally, as a short-run measure, we have urged the government to take steps to provide new and extended insulation capacity in federal offices and residential buildings right across Canada. The government took up that suggestion more than a month ago and applied it to Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia. We asked that there should be a national program in this area. This would not only create jobs; it would help toward the solution of an almost equally important question, the conservation of energy.
These, Mr. Speaker, are concrete steps which ought to be taken by a government which is truly concerned about the right of Canadians to work and the loss to our economy resulting from a million Canadians wanting to do something but being out of work. It is not enough, of course, for a government to deal simply with unemployment. It must simultaneously set up a mechanism to plan the national economy. This is what has been done in Sweden, in West Germany, in Norway and in Japan. A policy which deals with inflation for a time, moves on to deal with unemployment and then switches back again, is not good enough. We must plan the economy in a rational way so as to minimize, in a modern market economy, the amount of inflation while maximizing the number of jolts available for those who want them. That is the real issue.
Our party is committed to maintaining the capacity of our people to realize themselves as responsible citizens in their communities and among their families, and the most effective way in which they can do so is by finding jobs. It is time the government showed more sympathy with that objective.
I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles):
That the motion be amended by adding at the end thereof the following words: "This House also urges that the government
(1)	immediately decrease personal income taxes for those in the lower and middle incomes to stimulate purchasing power and take up the current slack in the economy,
(2)	immediately reactivate all federal capital works projects and encourage the provinces and municipalities to follow suit, and at the same time, lift any restraint on shared funding of such projects,
(3) immediately expand-in consultation with the provinces-the capital budgets for low income and co-operative housing and land assembly,
(4)	immediately launch an assisted repair and renovation program of homes owned by pensioners, the disabled and low-income families, and
(5)	immediately launch a program-in co-operation with the provinces-of insulating or improving the level of insulation in all residential buildings-a program which would provide not only jobs but would also conserve energy."
February 10, 1977

Canadian Human Rights Act
The United States privacy act and part IV of Bill C-25 have the same basic objectives. Both acts have basically the same approach to providing access through the creation of a federal index of personal information banks. Both acts provide for an individual to see his file and to propose changes if the individual feels that errors exist. Both acts provide for administration procedures to warn users of the file that the subject of the record objects to particular information in the record if an institution refuses to make corrections.
There are, however, certain differences which lead me to believe that the protection afforded under this bill of the rights to Canadians with respect to abuse of their personal information in government banks is effectively greater than the rights of Americans. Under the United States act, the non-elected head of any agency can decide whether an information bank is exempt from access. Under Bill C-25, it is not a bureaucrat but an elected minister who, in the case of a whole information bank, must first obtain the approval of the governor in council before any exemptions from access can be granted. Moreover, under the United States act there are certain blanket exemptions. An entire information bank can be exempted just because it belongs to the Central Intelligence Agency. In Canada, access to the data banks of the most sensitive agencies is not automatically excluded.
As a further safeguard against administrative or other abuse of personal information in government files, the bill requires that a member of the human rights commission be appointed privacy commissioner, with the power to review at public expense any complaint by any individual that he or she is being denied rights under this part of the act. Like the Auditor General or the Official Languages Commissioner, the privacy commissioner would be independent of the government and would report at least annually to parliament, and could include-and under the act is empowered to include-in his report accounts of individual cases where an error or injustice is not rectified. This approach is consistent with our parliamentary system of responsible government. It rests the ultimate responsibility for decisions concerning access to personal information upon the minister responsible to parliament. Establishing the office of privacy commissioner will make the government more accountable to parliament and, through parliament, to all Canadians.

However, we will be expecting, particularly on the privacy part of the bill, substantial amendments at the committee stage. Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to speak on Bill C-25 which is an act to extend the present laws of Canada which proscribe discrimination and protect the rights of individuals.
I believe the Canadian people should know exactly what we are establishing here. This is a bill to provide for a Canadian human rights commission, and the powers and functions of the commission are described. It is provided, for instance, that full-time members of the commission are persons deemed to be employed in the Public Service of Canada for the purpose of the Public Service Superannuation Act and for the purpose of the Government Employees Compensation Act and any regulations under section 7 of the Aeronautics Act. Also the commission is to provide for the payment of witnesses' fees to persons appearing before tribunals, and a tribunal may award compensation in the manner prescribed to a victim of a discriminatory practice.
I am not a supporter of establishing another government department or of expanding the bureaucracy, but certainly 1 support the establishment of the human rights commission. I want to read into the record this afternoon some of the reasons why we need such a commission and also to relate some of the discriminatory ways in which some employees are being treated by Crown corporations.
The enforcement of human rights legislation has always been weak and difficult. The Canadian human rights commission will have the exclusive power to turn away a complainant if it thinks the problem can be solved elsewhere. It could shortly become the last resort for a complainant as a result of overwork. The individual may be forced to turn to other agencies or even the courts.
The cases I am going to discuss this afternoon, Mr. Speaker, are cases that have gone to the court but the individuals have still not been informed why they were dismissed by the Crown corporation concerned. The individual or group has no right of appeal should the commission refuse to take a complaint or decide it is without basis. Nowhere in this provision does it state that the complainant has the right to information collected by the commission during the course of the investigation. The enforcement of a person's human rights is entirely in the hands of the human rights commission. I think there should be some check on what they do or refuse to do, and I hope this aspect will be thoroughly discussed at the committee stage.
In terms of enforcement, the commission has no powers. It can at any stage after the filing of a complaint appoint a tribunal which will hold meetings to determine whether the act has been breached. If so, it issues binding orders which are enforceable in the same manner as an order of the Federal

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, first, I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Schellenberger) for moving this motion today. It is one which should receive the full attention of both this House and the government, and I hope today's debate will result in action on the part of the government.
The problem which the hon. member has outlined with particular reference to the Panarctic inquest has brought the circumstances into focus. It is one which has existed for a long time, however. From time to time accidents take place involving people from different provinces. Inquests are held, and while attendance at those inquests is often arranged voluntarily, from time to time this is not possible and testimony which is vital to a fair conclusion is missing. The basic difficulty is that there is at the moment no power to compel attendance of prospective witnesses who are outside the province or territory in which the inquest is being held.
The Supreme Court of Canada has held in a recent case, Faber v. The Queen, 1976, that a coroner's inquest is not
3024

February 14, 1977
Inquests
criminal in nature, but civil. Accordingly, there is no federal jurisdiction with respect to the compelling of attendance by witnesses at coroners' inquests. At present, civil rules of procedure in each province empower a provincial court to issue a commission to take the testimony of a person or persons resident out of the province if this testimony is deemed necessary for a civil suit within that province. This, however, is the kind of process which is subject to many delays. It is not the sort of legal process which you would want to have in order to obtain the evidence of witnesses while their memory of an incident or of an accident is fresh in their minds.
It is essential for the efficacy of the inquest procedure that witnesses come before the inquest as soon as possible after the accident. There has been a move in Canada to achieve uniformity, and the uniform law conference has recommended a draft interprovincial subpoena act. I understand that this legislation has been adopted in Manitoba, British Columbia, Newfoundland and the Northwest Territories. Although the model act does not contain provisions per se subpoenaing witnesses to coroners' inquests, it nevertheless contains sufficient flexibility to allow the law to be amended to include that kind of proceeding as well as proceedings before bodies other than normal court bodies. It is this sort of approach which, I am convinced, will produce the kind of result which the hon. member is seeking in advancing this motion today.
Since I am strongly in favour of what he is suggesting, I do not want to hold up the proceedings any further. I urge the government to listen to what has been said today, and I urge the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) to include this question on the agenda of his next meeting with provincial ministers of justice, to push for the adoption of the suggested draft interprovincial subpoena act of the uniform law conference, and to urge that this act include the flexibility necessary to permit the subpoenaing of witnesses not only to coroner's inquests but also before other bodies.

I. The government has agreed to contribute $1 million through the Programme for the Development and Demonstration of Pollution Abatement Technology (DPAT) to St. Anne Nackawic Pulp and Paper Co. Ltd., to reduce air pollution problems from their Nackawic Mill.
2.	Since January 1, 1974, many air pollution studies have been undertaken in New Brunswick. A list of these studies is appended.
3.	Acres Consulting Services Ltd., has been engaged to conduct an air pollution study of emissions from the heating plant at CFB Gagetown, New Brunswick. Cost of the study was $25,000. Information collected is available to the public on request.
Air Pollution Studies Involving Environment Canada in New Brunswick since January 1, 1974; 1. Saint John Region Air Quality Study: This study was designed to follow up on the recommendations of the Lorneville Impact Study which assessed the effects upon air quality of the Coleson Cove Generating Station. It involves a monitoring network of six air quality stations and a program of computer modelling of atmospheric dispersion. It is hoped that the end result will be an aid to regional use planning and to the provincial air pollution control agencies. This study is being carried out in conjunction with Environment New Brunswick. 2. Air Pollution Assessment of Heating Plant at CFB Gagetown: Complaints have been received about emissions from this heading plant and a study is being carried out by a consultant under our supervision. 3. Air Pollution Study of Proposed Expanded N.B.E.P.C. Generating Station at Dalhousie, New Brunswick: This study was carried out at the request of the provincial department of the environment. Its purpose was to estimate ground level concentrations resulting from the proposed expansion of this generating station. The results were forwarded to the provincial department of the environment. The study involved computer modelling of dispersion from the stacks of the station. 4. Air Pollution Study in the Vicinity of the Lead Smelter at Belledune, N.B.: This study, also carried out at the request of the provincial government, involved computer modelling of dispersion of lead and particulates from the smelter. Much effort went into determining the emission rates at the smelter. At the present time the provincial government is carrying out an ambient air survey in the vicinity of Belledune, and the department is assisting them in the analysis of the samples that they are gathering. 5. Abatement Program, CIL Dalhousie Chlor-Alkali: This is not a study as such but is a program designed to ensure that the company is in compliance with the federal mercury emission limits to the air whose effect date is mid 1978. The department's activities there include inspections of the plant and meetings with plant personnel. 6. Lead-Free Gasoline Sampling: The department has an on-going program of sampling of lead-free gasoline in the Province of New Brunswick to ensure that federal regulations are met. The purpose of the regulation is to reduce emissions of lead from automobiles. 7. Leaded Gasoline Regulations:

The department takes quarterly samples from all refineries in New Brunswick to ensure that the leaded gasoline also meets the federal standards for leaded gasoline. Quarterly reports of lead usage are also compiled from the refineries. This is also intended to reduce emissions of lead to the atmosphere. 8. Evaluation, Inspection and Approval of DREE Funded Projects: This is an on-going activity whereby our department in co-operation with the New Brunswick Department of the Environment assesses the pollution aspects of DREE funded projects to ensure that they are not a cause of pollution. Funds are withheld until both federal and provincial agencies are satisfied. This aspect of the work involves much travel, inspection of installations, assessment of plans, etc. This activity is intended to prevent pollution from new sources. 9. EPS/AES Sulphate Monitoring Study-Eastern Canada: The purpose of this study which is just getting underway is to assess the importance of pollutants, primarily sulphates, heavy metals and nutrients, that may be transported over long distances, say from the Eastern Seaboard of the United States, and deposited here in the Maritimes. Some intensive monitoring was undertaken in August 1976 and it will be resumed by Environment Canada for a two year period beginning April 1, 1977.
There are other programs within DOE that are not specific to New Brunswick but which nevertheless are intended to alleviate air pollution there. These are as follows: 1. Development of Federal Air Emission Air Guidelines: Guidelines have been developped for the cement, asphalt and coke oven industries and others are being developed for the petroleum refining, pulp and paper ferrous foundries, non-ferrous foundries and iron and steel industries. These guidelines are available to the provincial air pollution agencies, including N.B. which they may adopt as regulations as they see fit. 2. Training of Provincial Personnel: DOE holds several courses a year in which provincial air pollution personnel are trained in the technology. 3. Training Operators of Federal Boilers and Incinerators with Respect to Air Pollution Control: The department intends to start this program this year in order to reduce air pollution from these installations. Training of operators in New Brunswick will be included.

It includes the anticipated supplementaries.
It includes not only the Main Estimates of $44,142 million which I am tabling today, but also reserves of $1,850 million for the supplementary estimates which may have to be tabled in the course of the fiscal year; and the aggregate of these two figures has been adjusted to take into account the customary lapses in credits voted, which are conservatively estimated at $872 million.
The Main Estimates proper include $41,145 million for budgetary outlays, the bulk of which will finance programs which are essentially redistributive in nature.
Many Canadians still have the notion that the money they pay in taxes to the federal government serves mainly to finance huge bureaucracies and remote agencies. Yet the operating and capital expenditures of all federal departments and agencies are expected to account in the coming fiscal year for less than one third of budgetary estimates, namely, $12.9 billion; and this includes the $3.8 billion required for National Defence.
I hardly need to remind hon. members that public servants, like other Canadians, spend most of their income on consumer goods, and that the federal government as my colleague the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Goyer), can attest-is the largest single customer of Canadian industry; so that what

we will spend on goods and services during the coming fiscal year will sustain, as in previous years, output and employment in the country's private economy.
But the point I wish to make, Mr. Speaker, is that almost 69 per cent of the budgetary expenditures forecast for 1977-78 will not really be "spent" by the government, in the sense that these moneys will not be used to pay the salary of public servants, or to build new federal buildings, or to buy furniture, paper clips and typewriters for government offices, tanks or planes for the Armed Forces, uniforms for the RCMP, and so forth.
Over $26 billion worth of so-called government "spending" will actually be paid back to individual Canadians in the form of social security payments, grants and subsidies, or transferred to their provincial and municipal governments, or used to pay interest to government bond holders, the vast majority of whom are Canadians. Therefore the federal government will directly plough back into the Canadian economy more than two-thirds of tax revenues and borrowings required to finance its budgetary expenditures during fiscal year 1977-78.
The same can be said of the $3 billion dollars required for non-budgetary outlays. These will be used to make investments in Crown corporations and to extend loans or advances to various departments and agencies such as the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, the Export Development Corporation, the Federal Business Development Bank and the Farm Credit Corporation. Consequently the bulk of the federal government's non-budgetary outlays will indirectly finance private expenditures such as housing, business and farm investment, or exports of goods and services.
I should point out that the 1977-78 Main Estimates include for the first time all non-budgetary items which are expected to be made under existing legislation, as well as those which must be included in appropriation bills.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would like to draw the attention of hon. members to a further dimension of the Main Estimates, namely, the manpower requirements of the public service during the next fiscal year. You will recall that my predecessor announced in the fall of 1975 the government's determination to curb and eventually stabilize the growth of the federal public service. The percentage increase of authorized manpower resources was reduced to 4.1 per cent in 1975-76; and the ceiling on public service growth was drastically lowered to 1.3 per cent in 1976-77.
A thorough review of manpower requirements in departments and agencies has enabled the government to project the growth of the public service at a still lower level in 1977-78- in effect, virtually to stabilize it. We have set the maximum level of authorized man-years in departments and agencies under Treasury Board Control at 323,272 in the new fiscal year-an increase of 2,081 man-years, or about six-tenths of 1 per cent, over the 1976-77 Main Estimates level. This is close to the "zero growth" target which has been suggested by some in recent months; but it has been achieved through successive assessments and reassessments of just what minimal manpower requirements were in each department or agency, rather than
February 16, 1977

through the setting of an arbitrary target for the public service as a whole, or the imposition of across-the-board percentage cuts.
We have thus been able to streamline the public service without impairing its ability to produce and deliver essential services; and we will press on, in the new fiscal year, with improvements in public sector productivity, notably through better and more extensive measurement of performance.
I hope to have established, Mr. Speaker, that the government is in firm control of both the public treasury and the public service. In the framing of our expenditure plan for fiscal year 1977-78, we have taken steps to make that control more effective; and we will continue to do so during the next budgetary planning period, which has already begun.
Restraint must not be confused with stagnation. The government must continue to respond to essential public needs. But it must ensure that its expenditure planning is responsible as well as responsive.

Mr. Speaker, I understand the concerns and the sentiment which the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Schellenberger) is endeavouring to bring before the House in the form of this amendment. I do not in any way wish to stifle his opportunity to discuss those concerns, which I am sure he holds very sincerely. However, the amendment he
3120

February 16, 1977
Advance Payments for Crops
has presented in the form of motion No. 2 is in danger of being out of order.
I would refer Your Honour specifically to the royal recommendation. In its own words, it recommends "the appropriation of public revenue under the circumstances, in the manner and amounts and, for the purposes set out in the measure entitled "An Act to facilitate the making of advance payments for crops." The only mechanism specified in the legislation for accomplishing the purpose of that recommendation is to provide for the availability of cash advances through the auspices of farm organizations. This is clearly explained in the definition clause of the bill and, later on, in some of the clauses dealing with the mechanism to be used. In other words, cash advances to producers of the crops defined in the legislation would be available through farm organizations. This is clearly the intention of the bill.
The hon. member's amendment seeks to depart from that principle by providing that cash advances, or loans as they might be called, I suppose, in layman's language, should be available not only through farm organizations but under other arrangements subject to a government guarantee. This is really quite a different principle from that outlined in the bill, wherein it is stated that cash advances may become available only where farm organizations are involved. This is clearly set out in clause 4(1). I will read the opening words: "Where an organization proposes to make an advance to a producer-", and so on. The hon. member's proposed subclause would go beyond the provision set out in clause 4 and would provide that individuals would be in a position to secure advances without availing themselves of the services of a farm organization. It goes not only beyond the terms of the legislation as presently drafted, but beyond the terms of the royal recommendation, for which reasons I respectfully submit it is out of order.
I do not wish to stifle the hon. member's opportunity to present his views on the subject, but I suggest that at a later stage he will have an opportunity to express his concern. Unfortunately, he might not be able to present his views at this stage, because the amendment he proposes is, I suggest, out of order.

When that doesn't work, of course, people crushed by law have no hope but from power, and if laws are their enemies they will be enemies of the law. Those who have much to hope for and nothing to lose will always be dangerous, and it is only when they are dangerous that sometimes we bravely get progress, because man climbed out of the slime because of discontentment.

Of course what really grew out of that thought was that freedom, in our understanding of the word, flows from the rule of law, not from people.
The Reformation, of course, brought sharply to the fore the need for the protection of freedom of religion. It is interesting to note that we got freedom of religion in Canada before the Mother Parliament adopted freedom of religion in the United Kingdom.
As the concept of the social contract theory of government developed in the 19th Century, still greater emphasis came to be placed on the rights of the individual. If the government failed to respect natural rights, wrote Locke and Rousseau, disobedience and rebellion were justified. Thus was born the modern notion of human rights. In this connection it may be useful for me to go over a review which Statistics Canada conducted in 1975 of the statistical legislation of other countries. The review concentrated on five countries, the United Kingdom, France, Sweden, the Federal Republic of Germany, and the United States. All of these countries have well developed, highly sophisticated, national statistical programs, and all have one or more pieces of legislation which regulate the collection, compilation, analysis and publication of statistical data by their respective statistical agencies. It is clear from this review that all of them rely, for the continuing viability of their operations, on some form and extent of mandatory reporting, although like ourselves they do not use this as a stick with which to beat respondents.
In the United Kingdom, for example, the legislation which governs the operations of the business statistics office contains a provision for undertaking legal action against non-respondents to official surveys of business establishments, with a maximum fine of $125 for a first offence and up to $500 for a second offence.
In France the legislation governing their Institut National de la Statistique et des Etudes Economiques also contains provisions for a penalty of up to $500 for a first offence for businesses which refuse to respond to official surveys. If a firm
February 22, 1977

is convicted of a second offence within a three-year period, the fine is increased to a minimum of SI,000 and a maximum fine of up to $5,000. In addition, special penalties can be assessed against large firms, that is, those with more than 100 workers. Upon conviction for a second offence within three years, they are liable to fines of from $10 to $50 per employee up to a total maximum fine of $10,000.
In Sweden also persistent non-respondents to official surveys of the National Bureau of Statistics are liable to prosecution at the request of the national bureau under king-in-council decree. If convicted, non-respondents are liable to a fine of up to 500 kroner, or approximately $125.

The first matter I want to deal with is the government's failure to ensure that the increased prices being charged Canadian consumers are in fact used for the purpose of discovering and developing new supplies of oil and natural gas. In the past four years the price of gas has doubled and the price of crude oil has increased three-fold. The petroleum industry and the government have consistently maintained that

these increases in price are necessary to ensure the cash flow needed to stimulate exploration and development. What has been the result? We are seeing a continuous decline in exploration.

The federal government will get nothing; the balance will go to the producing provinces. On page 38 of the energy strategy study we find this illuminating statement:
Current estimates suggest that with existing fiscal systems and prices that gradually increase towards current international levels, the industry will retain, after taxes and royalties, in excess of $3 billion per year (in 1975 dollars) on the average, over the next five years.
If ever there was a windfall, this is it. The government has repeatedly assured the House that it would monitor these windfall revenues paid to the oil industry by the consumers of this country so as to ensure that these moneys were used for exploration and development. The government has consistently over the years refused to follow the course advocated by the New Democratic Party, namely, that all the additional revenue from the rise in oil prices, except that part which goes to the producing provinces, should be retained by the federal government in trust for reinvestment in exploration and development. A popular move. A great deal has been said on this subject and I am happy to say a few words, partly to learn a few things about the subject that I did not know before, in the hope that it will be resolved once and for all and we will not have concerned elderly people worrying about what is going to happen.
In my short experience with perpetual bonds I have discovered that most of our predecessors who have spoken on the subject have regarded them with some amusement, saying "Oh, that old thing again, the good old perpetual bonds". At the same time, I think it is a fair impression that these bonds have been of real benefit to Canadians over the years. However, their day seems to have come. The history going back to 1936 was well covered by the previous speakers. As well as the original provision for calling these bonds, such as 60 days' notice, some provision to call them by lot is necessary if only some of the bonds were called, and also some measure to try to protect the bond holders.
As we know, in September of 1966 new bond certificates were issued for 30 years. To go back in history, these bonds have had their ups and downs in market value, but mostly down. Apparently the bonds did go up a little after the war, but that was for a very brief time. Within recent years, interest rates in Canada and elsewhere have risen to higher levels. This

February 28, 1977
Perpetual Bonds
has made them rather unpopular in terms of the lower interest rates which originally applied.
With regard to the motion moved by the hon. member for Don Valley (Mr. Gillies), it seems to me that one important aspect is the problem of the distribution of bond holders. That seems to be a very complicated proposition at the moment. However, if we can say one brief thing about that, there seems to have been a substantial change in ownership of the registered bonds since 1966. Since 1936 that change in ownership has been almost complete, so perhaps this mitigates a little the concern for the older bond holders not making it to the final date of 1996.
I understand also that there is some concern about there being a difficulty for the taxpayer in the proposal before us. The government has had a great deal of advantage from having these funds over the years, but it is considered somewhat difficult to ask the taxpayers-many of whom do not have investments of any kind, such as bonds and others-to bear additional interest costs in order to benefit those investors who bought bonds on their own initiative way back in 1936 and since then. It is even more difficult to justify the fortuitous benefit that would be derived by the vast majority of present holders with regard to the change in ownership that I just mentioned.
From the government side, how practical is the motion put forward by the hon. member for Don Valley? There are a number of concerns on the government side. First, there is the problem of trying to identify the original purchasers. Second, there is some problem with discrimination in the proof of purchase. There are problems concerning those bond holders who are deceased and the role of the successors in holding the bonds. There is a problem with selling recently at a loss, which would occur with some people. There is the problem with the proof of ownership once it has been discarded. It would discriminate against those people and would be in favour of those who maintain their ownership. There are various problems with redeeming prices below par.
Apparently various governments have looked at this possibility from time to time. The hon. member for Don Valley mentioned that the United Kingdom has gone very heavily into this type of investment as part of its debt structure, and there are others. The conclusion that has been reached by most of them has been that it would not be in the nation's best interest to fix the maturity date on these obligations.
There is also a concern about setting a rather difficult precedent, an implication that once we take some action to protect the investors from the vagaries of the market there is some discrimination against all other investors. Contrary to what some would propose, this does not apply to the issue of Canada Savings Bonds.
Therefore we have come down to the present solution proposed by the government, which is this. Having regard to all the circumstances, and although not necessarily to the current advantage of taxpayers, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) announced on March 18, 1975, that the 1936 issue of perpetual bonds would be redeemed at par on September 15,

1996. The legal process will be completed by June 7, at which time the Government of Canada will be irrevocably committed by law to redeem the bonds in 1996. Prior to the announcement the bonds were quoted at $37.25 per $100 for a yield of 8 per cent in perpetuity. At the present time the bonds are trading at a price of about $50.75 for a yield of 8.02 per cent to maturity. This yield is now comparable with other long term Government of Canada marketable issues.

concern are the storage and loading facilities at the port of Saint John.

(a) Radiation at any level is considered harmful in some degree. However, fallout is not subject to domestic control at source and the available counter-measures carry their own adverse health consequences. Therefore, protective actions must be based on a balancing of risks. Radiological health effects depend on the physical and chemical characteristics of the radioactive element involved, their mode of entry into the body and their deposition and retention in specific organs. For tropospheric fallout, iodine-131 is the element of greatest concern; for stratospheric fallout, the concern is chiefly with strontium-90. For both, the principal mode of entry into the body is by the consumption of milk. The amount taken into the body via other foods, drinking water and air is relatively small. The maximum permissible levels in milk, as derived from the recommendations of the International Commission on Radiological Protection, are 2,000 picocuries of iodine-131 per litre and 400 picocuries of strontium-90 per litre. The corresponding maximum permissible levels in air are 300 picocuries of iodine-131 per cubic metre and 40 picocuries of strontium-90 per cubic metre. For the complex mixture of radionuclides in fresh fallout in air, it is estimated that the equivalent level for gross beta radio-activity is about 2,500 picocuries per cubic metre. On this basis, it is considered that for short-term transient fallout exposures, levels in milk should not exceed the above value. However, if a period of widespread, long-term fallout was in prospect, more restrictive levels, approximately W of the above, would be specified to conform with the recommendation of the International Commission on Radiological Protection relating to the continuous exposure of a whole population, (b) The relevant United States levels are expressed in different terms, but in application do not differ significantly. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency has recommended graded scales of action if the total intake of a radionuclide from air, water and food falls within certain ranges. Range III, which requires consideration of possible counter-measures (other than surveillance), is 100-1,000 picocuries per day for iodine-131 and 200-2,000 picocuries

per day for strontium-90. These levels relate to average intakes by members of a sample population and they may be further averaged over a period of one year to allow for transient fluctuations.

March 3, 1977
Adjournment Debate
Though Mr. Champion arrived in Canada in July 1971, a request for his entry, sponsored by his wife, was made on August 22, 1971. Before any of the formalities related to his request could be gone through, Mr. Champion moved several times without leaving any trace of his whereabouts or advising immigration authorities of his change of address. Only in January 1976 did he again get in touch with the immigration authorities with regard to his landed immigrant status. He was then advised that, to meet the requirements of the department, he and his dependents would have to get a medical. He took his medical on April 5, 1976, but his dependents did not until September 21, 1976.
The civil servants advised me that Mr. Carlton Champion and his dependents were granted landed immigrant status on February 25, 1977. If Mr. Champion wants a settlement grant, he must go to his local immigration centre and his request will be studied in the light of current rules. In view of the circumstances I have just described, in all sincerity I feel the department acted in good faith with Mr. Champion.

Mr. Speaker, I am glad to have this opportunity to raise once again a matter which is of great importance. I have mentioned this matter in this House many times. I have raised it in public and in committee.
Generally speaking, I have found agreement with this idea.
It is not a new one. It is one I have been pursuing for sometime, and I have been trying to get some response from the government. I have been trying to get the government to take the initiative whereby a good housing program can be put into place in the Northwest Territories, especially in the Mackenzie district. I have been advocating a good log housing program under which people can build their own homes in the Mackenzie district using a local renewable resource, namely, logs, which are in abundance, especially along the Mackenzie and in the Liard area. I think this idea makes sense for the simple reason that a good log housing program would make use of a local, renewable, natural resource. It would provide badly needed jobs, and it would also provide housing for people in the Mackenzie district.
I have described the area at other times in this place as a disaster area, and that it is. I know this because I have travelled in the Mackenzie district. I have travelled in many parts of the Northwest Territories for many years. As hon. members know, I canvassed door to door in my campaign to become elected to the House of Commons.
I am raising this question again because I have not been able to get a positive response from the department. As most people know, bad housing creates social problems. Children do not do well in school, young people in the family may not be able to hold jobs, there are health problems, and there are

mental health problems, especially, in a very, very, cold climate. For some time I have been advocating that the territorial administration, through the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, initiate a good log housing program in the Mackenzie district of the Northwest Territories. People there who already have good log houses know that they will last for 100 years or more. As a rule maintenance is minimal and, as the houses are generally well insulated, heating does not cost a lot. Not much training is needed for construction, and I think we already have enough people with the knowledge to establish a good program. The need is there the material is there, and the labour is there.
If the program were launched it could start by filling an immediate need of the legislature of the Northwest Territories. They have a table, they have chairs for the members to sit on, a mace, and recently a Speaker's chair was presented by the Parliament of Canada to the legislature of the Northwest Territories. But, Mr. Speaker, they do not have a building. I suggest a project could be launched through Canada Works, perhaps the Department of Regional Economic Expansion or some leftover funds from LIP programs, and a log building constructed to house the Speaker's chair, the table, chairs, and mace that the legislature already has. Maybe 50 or 100 years from now the people of the territories would want a different kind of building, but this would be a starting point for a log housing program.
I may be stepping out of line, Mr. Speaker, in suggesting that some of the municipalities in the territories change their regulations that forbid a certain style of log construction The decision is up to them, but I would hope, once it was shown that a good log house worked and fitted in with the environment, that the regulations would be changed.
I should like to ask the department what the government is doing about such a program. I am sure this is not the first time they have heard about it and I will see to it that they hear more about it in the future. Is the government doing anything about such an idea?

He said: Mr. Speaker, in speaking to Bill C-35,1 am pleased at the outset to thank all hon. members who participated in the debate on second reading and in the discussions of the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs. As was noted on these occasions, the provisions of the bill are important for all residents of Canada, especially for those who have earned social security credits in other countries but who are deprived of foreign benefits in the absence of international agreements. Now that a general consensus has been reached concerning these provisions, I trust that hon. members will want to give the bill speedy passage.
The constructive suggestions made by hon. members on all sides of the House in considering this bill are a matter of public record. I would therefore like to describe briefly certain of the measures which my department has taken in responding to them.

In addition to the public information campaign, to which I referred in committee, for conveying the provisions of the bill accurately to the general public, I intend to continue our efforts to inform fully all members of program developments. As a result of the arrangements for closer liaison between constituency offices and OAS regional offices which my department inaugurated last December, our regional directors report that the level of service to pensioners has improved and that GIS renewals are being handled more effectively. This is due in large part to the more prominent role being played by hon. members and their constituency offices in handling inquiries from pensioners. For its part, the department has improved its field services through the establishment of 76 itinerant offices. In combination, these measures have led to a more efficient resolution of pensioner problems and, in most cases, to same day replies.
My department intends to reinforce this link by providing program information to constituency offices, as we have done during the initial phases of this bill. I will, of course, continue to welcome the comments of hon. members on our progress in this area.
When the standing committee was examining the bill the other evening, one hon. member raised an objection to the fact that we require the pensioner to sign jointly with his spouse the application for spouse's allowance benefits. I undertook at that time to investigate whether a pensioner had ever refused to sign an application for spouse's benefits. Upon investigation we could find only one instance of a pensioner refusing to sign the spouse's application out of over 75,000 benefits being paid, and even this particular instance could well be justified since in some instances the fact that a spouse's allowance would be granted could result in lower GIS benefits for the pensioner. The dual signing requirement would therefore not appear to be a significant problem. At the same time there are good reasons for having this procedure.
The dual signatures give some assurance, first of all, that the couple are indeed married or have a common law relationship and are living together. The dual signatures also mean that we have the spouse's acceptance of the fact that his or her GIS may be varied downward in accordance with the rates payable under the spouse's allowance program. Therefore it would seem to be the best course to leave the matter the way it is.

It is also the government's intention to broaden the options feature under the GIS and spouse's allowance programs to provide compensation for reductions in Canada Pension Plan benefits and for cessation or reduction of alimony payments or of private carrier disability insurance payments.
GIS and spouse's allowance benefits are payable on a fiscal year basis and are based on income received in the previous calendar year. However, when a person suffers a loss of income due to termination or reduction of private pension benefits, GIS and spouse's allowance benefits may be recalculated on the basis of the estimated reduced income for the
March 9, 1977

current calendar year, thus allowing for an increase in these income-tested benefits.
Currently, the old age security regulations governing this issue do not include CPP/QPP survivors' and disability benefits, alimony or private disability insurance payments. My officials have recently reviewed this issue and have concluded that the option provisions currently covering annuity payments, unemployment insurance benefits plus superannuation and other private pension payments should also cover supplementary CPP/QPP benefits, alimony and private disability insurance payments.
I wish to thank the hon. member for Gatineau (Mr. Clermont) in particular for having brought the matter to the attention of the committee.
The government therefore intends to amend the old age security regulations so that the new option provisions become effective with the proclamation date of this bill. In the meantime, my officials will continue to study this matter with a view to clarifying whether other income items should be added to the list used to determine entitlement to income-tested benefits under the old age security program.

Time does not permit me to review all the helpful suggestions made and the efforts being deployed in following them up. The primary objectives of Bill C-35 are to permit international agreements, and to provide greater equity in the treatment of beneficiaries and consistency among the three tiers of the Canadian retirement income system. Therefore, in once again thanking all concerned for their contribution toward achieving these objectives-and assuring them of the continuing co-operation of my officials and myself-I would urge upon all hon. members the bill's speedy passage.

I believe that we should take the procedures of this House more seriously and more positively so as to ensure that they will be respected not only by all members of the House but by the community at large. Therefore, I was very disappointed that we did not have the benefit of some positive recommendations from the hon. member for Edmonton West when he spoke a few moments ago and had such an excellent opportunity to make them.
Another matter that should be explored, I believe, is greater discipline in the House. When motion No. 12 is brought before the House, considered, and eventually implemented, I hope that the matter of discipline will be debated, especially in view of what we have seen in recent months. One thing upon which there should be some deliberation and debate is the matter of discipline. Discipline is something which will be needed if the rules and regulations of parliamentary procedure are to work. If there is discipline the public will respect hon. members in their work here in the House. If we, as the representatives of the people, are to be true leaders of our communities and provinces in this House, we should have discipline, and that should show in our every word and deed. respect of the public at large for the work we are trying to do here would grow.
I realize that this could be a topic for considerable discussion. I do not want to get off the topic of the rules of the House by belabouring the point about discipline, but if we could see the recommendations of the committee which to date has worked many hours, we could consider them, approve them, and perhaps adopt them, and we would then be able to enjoy the respect we all want.
On the matter of the so-called late show, the proceedings on the adjournment motion, I agree with the recommendation of the hon. member for Edmonton West that those proceedings should be held at a more reasonable time. Those proceedings are important, and rather than having a late show, perhaps the proceedings could be held from six o'clock to seven o'clock, or from one o'clock to two o'clock just prior to the question period. The committee should seriously consider this so that we might have a more reasonable time in which to give all hon. members an opportunity to express themselves and to participate in that particular order of the day.
The matter of closure was touched upon. No one likes closure. No one likes to see it used, but it is there for a very good reason. In past months it has proved its effectiveness, and I for one am convinced of its usefulness. It is obviously needed. If parties and members do not want to be reasonable and serious about a proposition which is put before them, and if they are hell bent, so to speak, on delaying the proceedings of the House, then it is proper for any government to invoke closure.

I would indicate, as I have on previous occasions when motions related to unemployment have been raised pursuant to Standing Order 26, that the matter, being one of continuing and chronic concern, it is not, in my opinion, a proper subject of special debate under Standing Order 26. That language was repeated by me as quoted at page 2296 of Hansard for January 24, 1977.1 again refer hon. members to it.
In this particular situation there is, of course, an additional consideration; that is, it is one, as indicated in Standing Order 26(5), regarding which the Chair ought to take into account opportunities which are likely to present themselves for a discussion of the particular problem that is raised in the notice of motion given pursuant to the Standing Order.
In this particular instance I can scarcely ignore the announcement that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) will put forward a budgetary statement on March 31 and that the motion accompanying it will be debated for some six days.
I understand there may not be specific agreement about the exact timing of those days, but nevertheless the debate will, I am sure, follow either immediately or very closely thereafter and unemployment, naturally, will be a very large feature of that debate. Accordingly, for those two reasons I regretfully decline the application for allowing a special debate on unemployment at this time pursuant to Standing Order 26.

In rising to say a few words about the subject I am conscious of the fact that with the exception of the Minister of State for Small Business (Mr. Marchand) and my colleague the hon. member for the Northwest Territories (Mr. Firth), all the rest of the members of parliament-all 262 of us-are either immigrants or the decendants of immigrants. The United States has a population ten times that of ours, and if they permitted proportionately the same number of people to come to their country as we have permitted to come into Canada, they would be permitting anywhere from 1.5 million to 2.5 million people to come into their country. Mr. Speaker, I would be remiss in my duty if I did not thank the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock (Mr. Friesen) for providing the House an opportunity to discuss child-napping, a matter of most serious concern to Canadians. This question has concerned the federal government for some time. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) discussed the matter with the attorneys general of the provinces at the federal-provincial conference of attorneys general in October of 1975. At the end of their discussions at that 1975 conference the minister called on the provincial attorneys general to come forward with suggestions on how section 250 of the Criminal Code of Canada might be improved in order to deal with the problem of child-napping. As yet, not one of them has put forward a proposal.
There may be a temptation on the part of some to ask why the federal government does not go ahead on its own and change the Criminal Code. However, I am sure that most of us are aware that the Minister of Justice has an undertaking with provincial attorneys general that there will not be any amendments to the Criminal Code without consultation with them. This, of course, is quite proper since it is the provincial attorneys general who are responsible under the BN A Act for the administration of justice within the provinces.
In the meantime, five provinces have passed legislation to facilitate the interprovincial enforcement of custody orders, and three more provinces have such legislation at various stages in the legislative process. I must say that I welcome this because I think that to a very great extent this is a problem that is best dealt with by provincial legislation.
The criminal law is too blunt an instrument to deal with the problem-a problem which exists entirely within the context of the breaking up of the family. It would be nice if the proposals contained in Bill C-221 would do the job and bring an end to child-napping. But they would not. Indeed I would say on the basis of the experience I have had as a lawyer that no jury in the country would, with the potential of a life prison sentence, convict a parent for having taken his or her own child to another jurisdiction.
I suspect that one reason why the Minister of Justice has received no response from the provinces to his request of 18 months ago for proposals for a change in section 250 may very well be that the provincial governments, having studied the problem, have decided that the Criminal Code of Canada is a totally inappropriate instrument for dealing with this very disturbing problem. That would perhaps be why so many of them have chosen to go with the legislation I mentioned a moment ago.

Mr. Speaker, on March 7 I questioned the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) with respect to his policy regarding the importation of pesticides and herbicides from the U.S.A. by Canadian farmers for their own use.
This capitulation to the multi-national companies at the expense of the Canadian farmer was disguised as an environmental safety precaution. Moreover, the monitoring system which would ostensibly protect the farmer and ultimately the consumer will be headed by a toothless, bureaucratic body. Under the past system, some farmers were effecting real savings by banding together and going south of the border for their purchases of agricultural chemicals. This in turn forced Canadian distributors of the American products to cut their prices.
Suddenly we find that regulations under the Pest Control Products Act have been amended to revoke an exemption previously given to the farmers. This is supposedly the result of an in-depth study that concluded that the "own use" exemption was inconsistent with the intent of the act to ensure safe and effective pesticides use in Canada, apparently safeguards on imports by a producer for his own use were weaker than those on Canadian registered products.
The minister claims that protection of a domestic industry was only a secondary consideration. The move gives every appearance though of being a canny manoeuvre to impose an embargo on pesticides in favour of multi-nationals distributing their products in Canada through dealers.
Of Canada's 300,000 farmers, the minister claims that 2,000 will benefit from the monitoring system. From past experiences, I am skeptical. Studies, reports to the minister, negotiations with the companies, procrastination, will frustrate the farmer and increase his production costs, which can only be reflected in higher food costs to the consumer.
The minister admits that 99.6 per cent of prairie farmers already buy a Canadian produced and distributed product. Was the embargo called for by the remaining .4 per cent or by Ontario corn farmers? Not highly likely! The pesticide companies became acutely aware of the benefits accruing to farmers who imported their own chemicals. They were forced to lower their prices to offset inventory surpluses and to attract their customers back. They asked for action, and were of course satisfied. The minister cannot honestly believe, and expect us to believe, that the embargo will foster a truly domestic pesticide industry, one where the decisions will be made by Canadians, in the interests of Canada.
In a speech to the Ohio Pesticide Education Association, the minister admitted that almost all pesticides used in Canada

Does the minister have any evidence he would like to share that, under the present circumstances, new industries are going to proliferate in Canada? My suspicions are that this is just another way the govermment has allowed multi-national companies to gain more control over our country.
The farmers' practice of importing their chemical directly, at a lower cost, was deemed an inequity partly because farmers living farther from the border could not profit in the same way. I maintain that the real price inequity was created by the middlemen, the distributors of the chemicals in Canada. This embargo will leave pricing totally in their hands. March 16, 1977
Privilege-Mr. Baldwin
between myself and the minister. The right of members of this House to inquire about the expenditure of public funds is as old and as cherished as the institution itself. Our rights today are so limited that any attempt sensibly to diminish them further must be regarded with alarm and form the subject of such a question of privilege as I am now raising. I shall be very brief because the issue is plain.
The agreement in question provides that with respect to information gathered covering the potential illegal sales arrangements or considerations or activities of Boeing aircraft and all its subsidiaries in Canada there is an understanding reached between the ministers, between the two attorneys general, which covers this particular activity of the Boeing company. Part IV provides that except as provided in paragraph 5, which deals with taking criminal and other legal proceedings, all such information made available by the parties pursuant to these procedures, that is, the procedures for gathering information, and all correspondence between the parties relating to such information and to the implementation of these procedures shall be kept confidential by both parties and shall not be disclosed to third parties, including government agencies having no law enforcement responsibilities- which, of course, covers this parliament, the House of Commons and all its members.
This agreement is a solemn convenant between two high officials of two governments to operate as a gag rule to prevent knowledge of certain facts being brought to the attention of members of parliament. It is not enough just to have criminal proceedings taken. The Minister of Justice may have in his possession a large number of documents and a great deal of material and information. All he has to do is make a conscious decision not to go ahead with criminal proceedings or, if he does, to limit the information to very specific cases. Everything else can go into the shredder, and there is no way under those conditions in which members of this House can discharge their constitutional responsibility to make an inquiry as to what are the facts.

Single mothers are more and more tending to keep their babies instead of putting them up for adoption. We are dealing here with a very important piece of legislation, one that sets the tone for the kind of culture that is going to prevail throughout Canada. It has been said before, but nevertheless I remind the House that in 1976, 3,326 orders in council were passed, of which only 653 were published in the Gazette so that Canadians would know about them. This means that there were 2,673 orders in council, pieces of legislation, about which Canadians had no opportunity to know. As we all know here, ignorance of the law is no defence, but how in the world can a person determine whether he is breaking the law if the law is not published anywhere?
This is why the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin), and Senator Forsey in the other place, are doing such an excellent job in regard to confidentiality and secrecy of government. Even Hitler, bad as he was, published his decrees so that the people there knew what was happening. But this government-and perhaps all governments, federal and provincial are moving in this direction-is administering the law by order in council, not by the passage of an act.
A former prime minister set the tone when he said this:
Let us come to another point which I wish particularly to stress. I refer to the right set out in Magna Carta that no man shall be dispossessed of his rights without the lawful judgment of his peers under the law of the land; not the law as made by the Governor-in-Council, not the law as made by some unnamed and as yet unexisting body, but the law of the land as known to everyone.
I have already pointed out that 2,673 laws were passed in one year about which no one knew except those who drew them up, someone in the public service. He continued:
It is an essential principle of liberty and freedom that the law of the land should be known, that it should be so known that every man as he runs may read. The law should not be something which is to make its appearance in the Canada Gazette after some board or Governor-in-Council, not Parliament, has passed a regulation; it is something that should appear in the statutes of the country.
Surely that is a fundamental principle. The late William Lyon Mackenzie King said that during a debate in 1934, and what he said then is just as true today. However, at that time we had not reached such complexity of government as today, when most legislation is passed by order in council.
Immigration
I want to tell the House a story, a very simple story, to illustrate what the danger is here. Back in the 1970's a Chinese girl by the name of Pui Chan Inoue came to Canada. They lived in Vancouver for a considerable length of time, had three children, and then went to Japan. When they got to Japan she found that he already had a wife, so she packed up her belongings, took one or more of the children and returned to Canada. She landed in Vancouver, but no sooner had she done so than she was arrested because she did not have a visa. She could not get one from Japan, she could not get one from Communist China, the only passport she ever had was from Taiwan and she had never seen that country. As a result she was thrown in jail.
It fell to my lot, Mr. Speaker, to do something about this case, and I did not realize until I looked into the matter and worked with a number of young students how complicated was the Immigration Act at that time, as indeed, the proposed Immigration Act will be complicated.
