Mr. Speaker, I go along with the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Sharp) in one respect, but in one respect only. Like him, I was a bit surprised when my hon. friends of the Official Opposition, after raising the point of order about $1 items yesterday, put down the same subject in a motion for debate and vote today. But at that point my going along with the hon. member for Eglinton ends.
I do not agree that this is an unimportant issue, that it is a waste of parliamentary time. Nor do I agree that it puts the Speaker in any kind of awkward position, whether he thinks so
Dollar Items
or not. In my view, the issue involved in this motion is an issue of decades, perhaps of centuries, namely, the whole question of the relationship between parliament and the executive. Even if some day we get this issue solved and put on a proper basis, I hope we will not forget to talk about it, because it is very important to the functioning of parliament that that relationship be on a proper basis. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, when the vote is called at 9.45 tonight we shall be voting for the motion.
I suppose that what I want to say now will lead to the charge that I am dealing in trivialities; but as one who is concerned about the fine points of parliamentary procedure and also about the fine points of the English language, I wish those in the Conservative party who draft these motions would not forever split their infinitives. But they have done it again today when they use the words "to fully discuss". Surely they could say "to discuss fully". This gives me the opportunity to say that I am delighted that my French speaking friends in the House do not split their infinitives, even if I have to say that it is because they cannot do so. That is why we have it in French in an unsplit infinitive, "discuter a fond". Despite this what some may regard as a triviality, but which I nevertheless think is important, my colleagues and I are going to support this motion.
The hon. member for Eglinton suggested that the Speaker is put in a difficult position of some kind. I deny that completely. What was raised yesterday was a specific point of order which was narrowed down precisely to eight or ten $1 items in the estimates. What the Speaker has to rule on today is whether any of those items are out of order and should not be allowed as items in the supplementary estimates to be voted on tonight. Whatever ruling he makes, there will still be $1 items which may not be illegal or improper but the use of which is an abuse of the relationship between parliament and the executive, and that is what we are talking about today.
I think we have both the right and the duty to keep this issue alive. What we are seeking to do is to maintain the control of parliament over the executive. I say to my hon. friend that even if his constituents in Eglinton and my constituents in Winnipeg North Centre are not waiting for news of this esoteric debate, it is important to them that this parliament be a place where the executive is responsible to parliament. When an executive can short-circuit and short-cut the parliamentary process by the use of $1 items, it is, in effect, downgrading parliament.
This is particularly true, and has been even more serious, since 1968 than prior thereto. I pick that date because it is the date when we made the rule changes which included the process we now follow in the passing of estimates. Prior to that date, a $1 item could be discussed in full on the floor of the House. Now, estimates are shipped off to standing committees

March 22, 1977
Dollar Items
and they come back to the House for a pro forma vote and we have no chance of discussing these items on the floor of the House. That means that when tucked in the estimates is a $1 item which amends a statute or brings in a new policy or agency which we ought to have the right to discuss in ordinary legislation, we not only do not have that right at all, but a form of closure is imposed upon us.
I suggest that all of the things that are said about the abuse which is involved in the use of $ 1 items will still stand even if the Speaker in his ruling today says that some of the $1 items in the current supplementary estimates have to be cut out of those estimates. However, I am not one to make the same speech day after day, and I certainly do not intend to stand here this afternoon and make the same speech that I made yesterday afternoon. I suppose I could just say to hon. members, or to readers of Hansard, that they should look at pages 4159 to 4163 of yesterday's Hansard and there they will find my speech. Having said that, I suppose I could now sit down.

I want to make it clear, Mr. Speaker, that I take no objection to the right of Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition to bring forward the motion, but I do question their intelligence in bringing it forth at this particular time. The opposition parties get two voting days in a term, and it seems absurd to me, when we listen to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), complaining that we are not debating the issues facing the country today, that the opposition should come up with such as absurd proposition.
Members opposite cannot have it both ways. We understand the concern they feel about the rules, because we share it on this side. We are extraordinarily frustrated. Take a look at what this House of Commons has done since it reassembled. We have passed the grand number of seven pieces of legislation since we came back here in the fall. Look at the progress which has been made with other legislation: we have got hardly any legislation into committee. If one really wants to know what the House of Commons has been doing, all one has to do is examine those motions we have passed under Standing Order 43 in which we have congratulated the winners of the Stanley Cup, congratulated the winners of the skating championships and congratulated Her Majesty on the twenty-fifth anniversary of her reign. But we have not been dealing with the problems which face Canada. It is absurdities like the motion before us now, after a day on which we have taken part in a procedural debate on $1 items, which bring the House of Commons and parliament in general into the rather low repute in which it is now held by the public at large.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre says he disagrees with the priorities set by the government in its program. That is his right. That is why he is on the other side. No government program will ever satisfy members on the other side of the House. Indeed, there is never going to be a government program which will satisfy all the members on this side of the House, either, no matter who forms the government. The fact is that we have limited resources. The fact is that the government must make decisions. The fact is that the government must bring down the program to present to parliament for action. But this parliament is unable to act.
I do not presume to know the reason for this. At one time I could say it was because the Conservatives were riding high in the Gallup poll and it was to their benefit to ensure that no decisions were taken in parliament. And one can argue, looking at what actually happened when the Conservatives were riding high in the poll, that very little did happen in the House of Commons. Now that they are not riding so high one might expect they would improve their performance to show that
March 22, 1977

they do have some ability. But no: we find they are doing no better when they are down in the poll, either. So one can only assume that no matter whether they are high in the poll or low in the poll, they suffer from basic incompetence.

The precedents of this House, which go back a number of years, reveal that the procedure in relation to $1 items has been used in a wide variety of cases in the past. Those cases have sometimes been the subject of debate and consideration here. On other occasions they have not been so debated. I do not know if there is any particular point at this stage in running through those precedents.
It might be very instructive just to point out to the House the general categories into which those matters in the past have fallen. I think of such matters as vote transfers where $1 items have been used. I think of items dealing with granting programs of the federal government; dealing with the deletion of debts and so on. I think of items such as amendments to previous appropriation acts where the procedure with respect to $1 items has been used in the past. I think also of the extension of other legislation to deal with special and urgent circumstances, and this has already been referred to today. In some cases there were changes in legislation other than the appropriation acts themselves.
It is interesting to note that in the discussions today, and in all the discussions of of which I am directly aware in the standing committees where these specifics items were dealt with in detail, hon. members of the opposition confined themselves to a complaint primarily about procedure. They have not directed themselves to any substantial extent to specific or reasoned arguments about the merits of otherwise of the substance contained in $1 votes. We have had procedural arguments.

March 22, 1977
Dollar Items
We have not had substantive arguments, and it seems to me this was the point Mr. Speaker was getting at earlier today. In order for him to come to a reasoned and substantive conclusion with respect to any item which is in dispute with regard to $1 items, he would want to hear viewpoints from one side and from the other side of this House. He would want to hear from the opposition as to where they take specific exception to an item being dealt with as a dollar- item, and he would want to hear the government's defence as to why that particular item should be dealt with as a $1 item. On the basis of those arguments, Mr. Speaker would be able to come to a conclusion as to whether this is a proper procedure. In his ruling today Mr. Speaker emphasized that he did not have the benefit of those kinds of arguments, and therefore he was limited or restricted in coming to the decision which he handed down. He suggested to us a procedure to follow in the future in order to avoid that dilemma. As I said, I think that instruction from the Chair will be very useful in guiding the House in the future.
I think the essence of what Mr. Speaker said in his ruling applies with equal force to what has gone on in this House today, but more particularly in the standing committees as the particular items which have been complained about today and yesterday have been before those committees for consideration. However, what have we heard in those committees, and what have we heard in the House? Have we heard specific complaints about what may be wrong with the Export Development Corporation, what may be wrong with the National Design Council, or what may be wrong in any of the other eight or nine points which have been complained about? No, we have not heard specific objections about the difficulty the opposition envisages with regard to any of these points.
We have merely heard a complaint about procedure, and as these items come before us on allotted days in the House, and as they come before us in the standing committees, there are times when the estimates are being considered when the substance of these issues could be debated and when arguments either for or against could be put on the record, but despite the indignation we have heard from hon. members across the way today and yesterday they have not, in any substantial way, availed themselves of the opportunities they have had to consider these items in the standing committees to the extent to which they say they need to do that. I think that is rather revealing in terms of getting at what is the real motivation or objective behind the motion we are dealing with today. I think the answer must be obvious.
The real motivation is not a concern about what may appear in these $1 items, because no member has directed himself to the substance of the $ 1 items. That seems to demonstrate quite clearly that the objective is to stall, to delay, and to prevent the House of Commons from doing the work of the country. Having said that, I hope in the future there will be a more expeditious and co-operative attitude on all sides of the House in our efforts to do the work of the country, for which we were elected.
I know that all of us want to be guided by the very learned remarks of Mr. Speaker as to how he would like to deal with

the continuing discussion which we will, no doubt, always have about what is and what is not a proper item to be included in the so-called $1 items in the estimates. I hope that all hon. members will take the recommendations of Mr. Speaker to heart. I also hope that all hon. members from this day forward will conduct themselves in this place with a determination to do what we were elected to do, and that is to provide effective leadership for the country and to deal with the issues of Canada in a current and topical way.

If the parliamentary secretary will also do some reading and if he will look at the proceedings of the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates, on February 27, 1969, the report of the committee carried this resolution, which was my motion, which reads:

He went on to say that the hon. member for Edmonton West drew attention to the fact that even Liberal members of the committee supported this expression of concern. That is a fact, and one of the members who supported me in that observation is the present Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie). I agree with those members and I share their concern. I think parliament should be concerned about the unwarranted extension of so-called legislation by $1 items. Their own minister, the minister responsible for the introduction of supplementary estimates, states that he was concerned.
The Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council said, "Why does not the opposition argue the substance of those particular items?" What? Items that are illegally before the House? But there has been, at the same time, support for the continuing role of the federal government in providing financial support for provincial governments in essential services, particularly for provincial governments with a smaller than average tax base. I do not think anyone needs to apologize for this ambivalence. Partly, we oppose this bill because several provinces, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Prince Edward Island and Quebec, think certain services can be provided more cheaply and efficiently outside intensive care hospitals which are jointly funded by the federal government. Unfortunately those outside services are not funded by the federal government. The bill makes no provision in this regard, and that is partly why we think it is wrong. It will reduce minimum health service standards and the availability of post-secondary education which, so far, we have been able to provide to Canadians in all parts of Canada.
This year, pretty well every university raised its student enrollment fees. Now, since Ottawa is to cut back the proportion of money it makes available for university education, our universities must increase fees once more. As well, most provinces will face severe financial constraints. For those reasons we oppose the bill, as we opposed the change in the Medical Care Act. We shall oppose any changes to the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act. We oppose this kind of whittling away of basic and fundamental rights all Canadians have enjoyed for a quarter of a century. This whittling away can only aid the cause of separatists in all parts of the country, Quebec, Alberta or British Columbia.
If you cut back services, how can you make people believe it is great to be Canadian? Why should people in New Brunswick enjoy a lower level of service than people in Ontario and British Columbia? Because the people of Ontario or British Columbia live in provinces with resources fetching high prices now, surely that does not entitle them to infinitely better services than are available to people in Newfoundland or New Brunswick? That, fundamentally, is why we oppose this bill.
I do not want to repeat what I said at the second reading stage of the bill. However, I want to dispute vigorously the statement made today by the Minister of Finance, as well as the statements made by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) when we were debating this bill on
Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements second reading, that the provinces voluntarily accepted this bill, that they welcomed this bill, and that they will be better off as a result of it. The facts are, as our leader put on the record, that the premier of Alberta, speaking on behalf of all the provinces, made it clear to the federal government that all ten provincial governments, regardless of party, were opposed to the provisions of this bill.
The minister said that the provinces have accepted the bill. He implies that we are not telling the truth. Of course they accepted the bill. They knew that if they did not accept it, the funding which they have been getting for these programs under the old legislation would end. It had a time limit. They would not be entitled to any funding when the legislation would end this month. They had a choice between accepting this bill or getting nothing, because there would be no legislation in effect. They would have to depend on the charity and good will of the federal government. And they had sufficient experience with this federal government to realize that they did not want to be put in that position.
Let me point out what will happen to the provinces as a result of the passage of this bill. The province of Ontario will get $50 million in the next fiscal year, British Columbia will get $23 million, and Alberta $90 million. The poorer provinces stand to lose. Prince Edward Island will lose $2 million. Saskatchewan will lose up to $3 million. Manitoba will gain $800,000 the first year, but will lose money in subsequent years. That is only with respect to alternate care for adults who can be placed in institutions other than intensive care hospital beds.
The minister must not be permitted to get away with his statement that the provincial governments not only accepted this bill but will in fact be better off than they would have been had the bill not been passed. I want to put on the record the views of the two provincial governments with which we are in closest contact. Up to now, our assessment of the proposals in their ever-changing form is that they are not an adequate replacement for cost sharing commitments which had previously been made by the federal government. Our own calculations suggest that the per capita amounts offered so far would barely offset existing recoveries for Manitoba. And, they would not come close to matching the support levels that were anticipated under:
The 1975 offer to extend hospital and medical care sharing to cover alternative services, and the mid-1976 version of the proposed social services act.

Mr. Speaker, I do not want to delay the proceedings on this very much. I would like to speak for about two minutes. I have been concerned, as I am sure all members have, with the customs and the traditions of our law-shaping forces. We are, in effect, saying to the Canadian people, "This is good for you and you darn well better have it." This is not a new concern of mine. Indeed, in moving the address in reply to the Speech from the Throne in 1969 1 quoted with approbation an editorial appearing in the Sarnia Observer which read in part as follows:
The real threat to parliament isn't the possible danger of cutting off productive and informative debate on a measure, but the steady erosion of prestige by the tiresome speeches, lack of decorum, obstructionism and poor attendance in the House. The House of Commons is its own worst enemy and every time it aids its own weaknesses it chips away a little more of its own fabric.
As I said at the time my concern about the passage of legislation was that we were taking too much time, rather than too little, with our legislation. When we spend too much time and have so many speakers, do the speeches themselves lose significance? Invariably it is a judgment call that must be made about the amount of time that should be spent at any stage of a bill. For this particular bill I note that we have spent some 13 hours on second reading debate and we have heard 26 speakers from all parties argue for and against its proposals.
It seems to me that in order to approve or disapprove of it in principle, as we are doing at second reading, the time already spent and the time to be allocated under Standing Order 75C should be adequate. We have heard the opponents of this bill make the same arguments against its content, and those of us who favour its passage have stressed the good aspects of the bill. But surely there comes a time when a decision must be taken on the principle of the bill.
Close clause by clause scrutiny of Bill C-27 will take place at committee stage, there will be further debate on any amendments proposed by the committee at report stage and then we will have final reading. Many of the points raised by hon. members would most appropriately be dealt with at one of these other stages in the procedure.
In addition to the amount of time that has been, and will be, spent on consideration of the bill, we have the statements made by the member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) that if all changes he wants are not made he is prepared to filibuster the bill at all stages. Given the time we have already spent on the bill, the time to be made available, one hon. member's threat to filibuster and continue a monologue, 1 feel it incumbent on me as the minister to take my responsibilities and ensure that this piece of legislation continues to move fairly and reasonably through the parliamentary process.

This program makes sense in Nova Scotia and in Prince Edward Island, and there is no reason why it would not make sense in the rest of the provinces. [The Acting Speaker (Mr. Ethier).]
We would like to see the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Buchanan) bring in a bill next week announcing a major expansion of public works projects across Canada. If he could just put back on to the record the legislation he set aside when the period of restraint was inaugurated a year and a half ago, it would be supported by this party, and it could pass through the House of Commons. Projects of that kind would provide jobs right across the land.
There are a number of short-run proposals we think the government should act upon before we adjourn. We think there should be a tax cut, that the housing industry should be stimulated, and that there should be more capital works projects and assistance for urban transportation. There is nothing remarkably profound or innovative about these proposals. Anybody in Canada who is concerned about employment and simultaneously concerned about economic responsibility could advocate these proposals. A concerned government would not only have advocated them, but would have put them into the budget last night.
My party fully recognizes that the proposals I have just made are short run. Even if they were all accepted by the government and carried out, they would not create by the end of 1977 or 1978 anything approaching full employment. It would be deceptive to suggest that that would be the case, but they would constitute a major beginning which we did not get in last night's budget.
Before we adjourn we would like to see the government bring in a bill committed to creating full employment over a period of years and to setting specific targets. Last fall on behalf of my party I proposed such a program. It was the result of about a year's work by a number of people in my party. I will not present all the details of the program today in the House. I have done that before, but this program stipulates that if we had a government which was committed to serious action, we could indeed have virtually full employment at the end of a four-year period. That is precisely what the people of Canada want to see. They do not expect miracles. They do not expect a government which is faced with one million unemployed to come up with a program which, within six months or a year, would make all our problems go away. However, the people expect the government to make a long range commitment which is backed up by specific proposals, for example, to move from the misery of the winter of 1977 to a winter of perhaps some contentment four years down the road.
My party would like to see the government bring in a full employment bill which would set out specific targets, and which would make it mandatory for the minister to report to the House at least once a year justifying his targets for that year and explaining how government has or has not lived up to its targets for the preceding year. In short, we would like to see the government commit itself to long range planning with regard to employment and with regard to the economic situation in general.
I said a moment ago that the people of Canada do not expect miracles. They do not expect politicians to have simple remedies to complex problems, but they do like to see a

government which recognizes the complexity of an issue, which recognizes the complexity of the nature of the Canadian economy, and which suggests how to get out of our current structural problems.
In addition to what I said about a full employment bill, my party also believes the government has to do something about the problem of economic independence in Canada. We believe that the problems of the Canadian economy are inextricably connected with the fact that the vast majority of our material resources are owned and controlled outside our borders. With a government like this and a budget like that produced on Thursday night, it is no wonder that we have a generation which is being schooled in cynicism and hopelessness? This dismal budget begs any number of questions, but no question is more fundamental than the simple one: Why, given the very real problems facing the Canadian economy, would the minister choose to give us a budget that addresses none of these problems? Why, given the current need for some sense of certainty and reassurance, would the minister offer the country only new confusion and new uncertainty? Perhaps the most direct and, indeed, kindest explanation is that this government is simply too incompetent to deal with the country's problems. There is no lack of evidence that this government has long since run out of any steam that it ever had.
Another possible explanation is that this government in fact has a very limited view of what this country can achieve, a very limited view of the possibilities of Canada. It does not seek to achieve our growth potential as a country because it does not really think we have any. It really is not seized with the problem of one million unemployed Canadians-with more coming, thanks to this budget-because it accepts unemployment as a norm for Canada. Besides, do we not have a generous unemployment insurance program in this country? This kind of reasoning can cause us to lose forever the chance

April 5, 1977
The Budget-Mr. Lessard
to achieve the potential of this country. If that, indeed, is the view of this government-and there are plenty of musings from the Prime Minister to suggest that it is-then, bluntly, this government is simply not worthy of this country. This country, with all its potential, deserves much more than a government whose highest ambition is to stand still. The people of Canada deserve better than a government which sees the Canadian dream as being two parts unemployment insurance and one part welfare.
There is a third possible explanation for this budget, Mr. Speaker, one so cynical that I would not attribute it to any government but this one. It is that the minister's budget decisions were made on the basis, not of Canada's economic needs but of the Liberal party's electoral strategy. If there is to be no election in 1977, then why waste any effective action this yeaf? Next year is when the government needs the "goodies". So one million Canadians will just have to wait until Keith Davey gives them the green light.
As I say, Mr. Speaker, I would not even suggest such a cynical approach by any government other than this one. But I look back at this government's economic policies and I ask myself whether they have ever had any basis other than sheer political opportunism. In 1968, in that famous election campaign, the Prime Minister went around the country-this should be remembered in light of his record-telling Canadians that it was time to "end the free stuff'. That from the right hon. member for Mount Royal! Then he went on the wildest spending binge in Canadian history.
In 1974 the Liberal campaign strategy-their "promise for tomorrow"-was to point out of television sets at Canadians and say, "Zap, you're frozen", and then to introduce the very controls regime that they had attacked. Canadians, looking at that record, will ask themselves whether this government is not capable of putting aside the needs of Canada if they do not happen to fit in with the plans of the Liberal party. I will let this House and the country decide which of those explanations best fits this unworthy government. Canadians can decide whether this government is simply incompetent, whether it has no faith in Canada, or whether it is just too cynical to care. Canadians can make that choice, Mr. Speaker, for these questions all lead to the same conclusion. There is simply no justification for this government to remain in office, and the sooner Canadians get their right to change that, then the better for all of us.

Mr. Speaker, pursuant to the provisions of Standing Order 43 I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. In view of the urgent need for employment opportunities in the Placentia-Argentia area of Newfoundland and the opportunities that would be created once the facilities on the north side of the U.S. naval station Argentia are turned over to control by Newfoundland authorities, and in view of the fact that the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson) one month ago advised the mayor of Dunville that the U.S. government is prepared to lease back to Canada the unused properties and that he hoped there will be created a Canadian management authority in the area but that formal negotiations should begin only within the next two or three months, after a period of unnecessary delay,
I move, seconded by the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Howie):
That the Secretary of State for External Affairs be instructed to treat the matter of obtaining of the facilities at Argentia by Newfoundland as a matter of urgent and pressing necessity, with negotiations to this end to be concluded immediately and the facilities made available for industrial purposes now, and that the Department of External Affairs make this their highest priority in United States-Canada relations.
